subsubtopic: SUGGESTION CANADIAN COMPANIES IN SOUTH AFRICA AND NAMIBIA ESTABLISH EQUALITY IN TREATMENT OF WORKERS- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. With respect to assertions at the United Nations this week that seven Canadian companies are collaborating with South Africa to exploit the resources of former Southwest Africa, and in view of Canada's continued rejection of South Africa's illegal occupation of Namibia, as well as our opposition to the practice of apartheid, and with regard to a recent initiative of 11 major American corporations with operations in South Africa to apply a set of guidelines ending desegregation in eating, toilet and working facilities and establishing equal pay for equal work in South Africa, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather):
(1)	That Canada declare its strong opposition to the support of Canadian business enterprises for South African involvement in Namibia,
(2)	That an inquiry be made to ensure that no tax advantages are provided to Canadian companies operating in Namibia,
(3)	That Canadian firms operating in South Africa be encouraged to pursue initiatives similar to their American counterparts in establishing clear guidelines and working conditions with the South African government which will establish equality in treatment for workers regardless of race.

important matters either by an agency of the House of Commons or by any other government agency unless specific charges have been made by a member of this House, and since there have been general charges made-and perhaps specific charges; we have not yet seen the list of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs against Radio-Canada by ministers of the Crown, is it the intention of the Prime Minister to instruct his ministers who feel they have charges to make, to make those charges to the CRTC specifically, and to make them public so that this House and the people associated with Radio-Canada will know of what they are accused, and by whom?

subtopic: SUGGESTION MINISTERS MAKE SPECIFIC CHARGES AGAINST RADIO-CANADA

speechtext: And documenting them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
That this House condemns the failure of the government to provide economic leadership and in particular its failure to introduce measures which will ensure economic growth and provide jobs for the more then 1,000,000 Canadians who need them; and calls upon the government, in its March 31st budget, to correct these failures by:
1.	establishing new direct job creating programs in needed social fields such as housing;
2.	reducing taxes for middle and low income earners; and
3.	assisting urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projects including rapid transit.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as the motion before the House makes clear, the Canadian economy, putting it briefly and accurately, is in terrible shape. Growth is almost non-existent, and as most in this House have finally realized, more than one million Canadians are without work. The situation is deplorable in terms of its effect on people. First and foremost, in Canada as elsewhere, ordinary people want to work, want jobs, want to contribute directly to the well-being of their families and communities. They prefer jobs to hand-outs: that is the human reality.
Second, the present situation is dangerously bad for the economy. Existing unemployment levels mean that we are paying some $2 billion a year in unemployment insurance and welfare; we are losing between $6 billion and $7 billion a year in production, since goods are not being produced; and we are losing at provincial and federal levels hundred of millions of dollars in taxes which would otherwise be paid by Canadians if they had jobs and were earning money with which to pay taxes. The result is that the rest of us, particularly middle and low income Canadians, have had to pay more taxes than would otherwise have been the case.
Bad though our circumstances are, it is important to know that the present malfunctionning of our economy, with its attendant high unemployment, is very bad for national unity. November 15 was the most important date in recent Canadian history. Its events were a sign of serious discontent in the country. But what they symbolized is not new. Economic grievances in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada have been building up for years: they have been ignored by the Liberals for precisely the same number of years.
Anxiety and conflict about the future of Canada are inescapably related to Canadians' sense of economic well-being, to their sense that our federalism is fair to themselves and their families, to their feeling that Ottawa, to put it bluntly, cares about them as people. How is it possible for young Quebeckers who are experiencing directly in their lives the reality represented in the statistic that more than 50 per cent of the new unemployment in Canada, as a whole, occurred in their prov-
March 8, 1977

ince alone, to feel an emotional commitment to the central government?
How is it possible for young men and women of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, that beautiful part of our country, 70 per cent of whom were unemployed according to a survey done last summer, to feel emotions of commitment to their national capital and central government? How is it possible for the more than one million Canadians in the regions in virtually every province, Canadians without prospects of employment, to feel a strong sense of identity with their nation's capital?
In circumstances such as these there is a tendency for Quebeckers to blame English Canada, for Canadians elsewhere to believe that Ottawa does too much for Quebec, and for virtually all other provinces in Canada to resent the province of Ontario. These are the precise consequences that occur in a diverse and large country like Canada when people, wherever they are located, have the accurate perception that they are being unfairly treated by the central government.
The point is that a sense of economic fairness in life's opportunities is inescapably related to feelings of national unity. The point is that the Liberals have persistently ignored this and, in particular, have been responsible for the current disgraceful level of unemployment. We need a real growth rate of at least 5.5 per cent just to maintain current levels of unemployment. Surely that statistic itself should be of concern to all Canadians. Just to stay where we are, with more than one million people out of work, we must have a growth rate of 5.5 per cent and we are not getting it-and the prospects are not better, they are worse. In the last quarter of 1976 we had a negative growth rate of .6 per cent.
With the current policies of the government, real growth for 1977 is estimated to be only about 3.5 per cent. I ask hon. members to keep that in mind and relate it to what I said a minute ago about maintaining existing levels of unemployment, let alone improving the situation. If we have a growth rate of only 3.5 per cent, and we need 5.5 per cent to keep one million or fewer unemployed, the conclusion is inescapable and distasteful: unemployment in Canada will get worse, not better. It means that government policies, if they are going to reflect the concern about the unemployed and concern about national unity, will have to change fundamentally.
The budget that is to be brought down on March 31 should, in the view of the NDP, contain the following set of proposals. I put them forward not in a dogmatic sense, not with the conviction that they are the only approaches that can get us out of our terrible economic mess, but in the sense that the government must adopt measures like these, if not these precise ones, if it is to show the concern that is required about the more than one million unemployed in the country and the concern across the land to bring about some sense of economic justice in order to promote national unity.
We say that the government must move directly in terms of job creation, and I will make some specific suggestions. First, they should immediately reactivate the federal capital works
Economic Policy
projects set aside during the period of restraint, and simultaneously encourage the provinces and municipalities to follow suit. With more than 145,000 construction workers unemployed across the land-that is the figure for January, 1977, the most recent data-this move would not in itself be inflationary. If people are out there looking for jobs, you will not put more pressure on the job market by providing employment. What you do is to provide the jobs and stimulate the economy.
Second, the government should immediately expand budgets for low income and co-operative housing projects. Third, it should immediately expand to all of Canada the insulation program for houses and apartments now in effect in only Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. When the government lifted this particular proposal out of our suggestions ma'de last October, we were delighted that they applied to two of our eastern provinces this sensible and practical proposal. What we say now is that the government should go all the way in adopting a good idea and extend it to the remaining eight provinces in Canada. This program would not only provide jobs but also conserve energy.
Fourth, the government should immediately tell our municipalities that its 1974 election promise to provide $290 million in financial assistance for rapid transit will be implemented. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said one day that it would not happen. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to the House three days later that it might happen. Then we have the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), presumably going back to the position of the Minister of Finance, saying no, he does not think it will happen. We say that that promise made sense in 1974. It was a promise to do something to assist our municipalities in rapid transit. It made sense in 1974, and it makes sense in 1977. In addition to providing jobs needed in the economy, it will constitute a conservation measure to reduce our consumption of oil, a measure which is long overdue. It is the kind of concrete step in federal assistance in a serious conservation direction which is long overdue. These are four concrete suggestions for direct federal involvement in job creation.
In addition, we believe that other steps are needed, particularly in the fiscal area. We recommend an immediate tax cut for low and middle income earners. We recommend that a $1.5 billion tax cut be brought into force immediately, to be complemented by the abolition of the indexation system, a proposal of the Official Opposition which the government foolishly and erroneously adopted. The step we are recommending is to have a tax cut of $1.5 billion for medium and low income tax payers and to abolish the indexation system, which will save about $1 billion for the treasury.
The net result would be an infusion of $500 million into the economy for those who most need it. We are saying specifically that the tax cut for medium and low income tax payers should be in the form of tax credits, with more money going to lower income people and less to upper income people. We are recommending, for example, that those with a taxable income of $5,000 should get a $400 tax credit, those with a taxable income of $10,000 should get $300 tax credit, those with

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
$15,000 should get $200, those with $20,000 should get $100, and those Canadians earning $25,000 or more a year should get no tax credit because they need nothing at this time in terms of a tax cut. Such a tax reduction would provide a badly needed stimulus to the economy and therefore would provide additonal jobs.
Earlier I indicated that I did not believe expanding by means of direct spending in the construction field would lead to further inflation. I said that this was obvious because there were 145,000 construction workers out of work. Let me add that the tax cuts which I am proposing would not be inflationary. I cannot understand the preoccupation of the Minister of Finance with the small "c" conservative economic advice that he is apparently getting which suggests that at this time there should be a trade-off between inflation and unemployment, and that if he stimulates the economy through tax cuts, there will be inflation.
At this time in the performance of our economy I suggest that that is nonsense, and I will tell the House why. At present, the manufacturing sector of the Canadian economy is operating at only 81 per cent capacity. That is an 11 per cent drop in three years. In 1973, stimulating the economy by means of direct tax cuts of the kind we are advocating could well have put inflationary pressure on the manufacturing sector that was operating at 92 per cent capacity, which was the case at that time.
However, now, when it is operating at 81 per cent capacity, stimulating by tax cut is not only the most immediate, direct way of creating jobs but it also does not provide any additional inflationary pressure on the economy. All that would happen as a result of such a tax cut is that existing plant, equipment and office space which is not being put to work now would become active, and idle men and women who are collecting unemployment insurance or welfare-or both-would have the opportunity to contribute some constructive labour to the community. That is precisely what we think ought to be done.
Having made these positive suggestions, I want to take this opportunity to say something about what ought not to be done. Given the past performance of the Liberal party, 1 am deeply apprehensive that it will move in the direction I am now going to discuss. Tax concessions to corporations are simply too expensive at this time, and more important and related to the argument, they would not be effective. Because of the high rate of unused capacity, tax concessions to stimulate capital investment would be ineffective unless they were so massive as to be a lot more costly to the government than other means of direct stimulation to create jobs in the demand sector of the economy.
Most economists are now agreed that tax concessions are not the best medicine at this time. That is not a view put forward exclusively by the New Democratic Party of Canada. As the C. D. Howe Research Institute said last December:
The case for additional tax concessions to boost investment in the short run is being considered mainly in the context of the weakness of this sector's contribu-
[Mr. Broadbent.J
tion to aggregate demand growth. But with the degree of excess productive capacity and the pervasive pessimism about the future that now exists, such concessions are unlikely to have as prompt, or as powerful, an influence on investment spending as some might think. Therefore, if a reasonably quick boost in demand is required, the chances are probably greater of getting it by stimulating private consumption.
In other words, by direct tax cuts to low and medium income earners who will almost automatically spend it. Let me add another comment from that category of economists who are not normally in wholehearted support of the kind of proposals made by the New Democratic Party. Mr. Bob Simon, director of taxation at Brascan, agrees with the argument 1 just made. Let me quote a succinct sentence which sums up his own argument. With reference to corporations he said: "People won't build until they need to". Unless there is a general, sufficient demand in the economy and a general, sufficient expectation that if businesses expand, their resources will be used, businesses simply will not act. This makes elementary economic sense. One would have hoped that the Liberal government learned this many years ago, and I say to the ministers who are here, for God's sake do not bring forward that kind of tax concession for corporations in the upcoming budget. If that is done, ordinary taxpayers will have to pay more as a result of corporations paying less, and we will not get additional jobs.
In addition to these short-run considerations, there is a great deal of evidence that tax concessions of the kind we now have permanently in place vis-a-vis corporations distort investment decisions by making the cost of capital artificially low compared with labour, and by favouring large, capital-intensive industries over smaller ones they in fact have an opposite effect to what is intended. Instead of producing more jobs in labourintensive sectors, from an economic point of view we encourage an irrational overinvestment of capital which leads to a reduction of jobs. That kind of long-range argument used to be made within the cabinet by Eric Kierans. I do not know of a present member of the cabinet who has enough economic and social sense to consider it. I hope someone is in there arguing, but I suspect there is not. On behalf of my colleagues, I repeat that argument today.
Beyond these important short-run steps of direct stimulation to the economy by job-creation programs and indirect stimulation by tax cuts which I have called for, we need a major long-run shift in policy. What we need is a commitment by the national government that a job should be available to every man and woman in Canada who wants to work. This goal is not the goal of the government of Canada, nor is it the goal of the government of the United States. It has never been a national objective of any government in North America. It is, however, the serious commitment of a number of social democratic governments in western Europe, and I suggest it is long overdue on this continent.
As far as we in the New Democratic Party are concerned, if a commitment is to be seriously made and seriously implemented, it would have to contain the following elements: first, we should have a full employment act passed in Canada. That act should recognize the right of Canadian men and women to
March 8, 1977

work. Full employment should be stated as a national and continuing objective. Second, and related to that, on an annual basis and as required by this proposed national full employment act, the government should have to bring before parliament its annual targets for job creation. It should set out in realistic terms the number of jobs it plans to create in a given year and in what sectors it is anticipated they should be created. Then at the end of the year the government should be obligated to review its own record of job creation, and those on the opposition side of .the House should be obligated to put the government to the test to see if it has lived up to its mandate.
Finally, as a further element of such a national strategy for full employment, the government should establish long-range targets. These targets should not just be annual; they should be for periods covering four to five years. On behalf of my party last fall I suggested that in realistic terms full employment could be achieved in Canada. I did not suggest it would happen next year or the year after, but perhaps four years down the road. It is as long and as serious a process as that, I am prepared to acknowledge; but we will not achieve it in this country unless the government commits itself to achieving such a goal and begins now to implement short-run strategies to bring it about.
Last fall we suggested that we could bring down the rate of unemployment 1 per cent per year over the next four years, so that in four years we would have an unemployment level not exceeding 3 per cent. That is virtually full employment when we take into account people who are voluntarily out of the labour market at any given time because they are moving, because they want a change, or for whatever rational, human reason. I repeat that what we need is a commitment of long-range proportions from the government of Canada to achieve a full employment policy.
In addition to the specific points that I think are necessary for long-range strategy, I would also assert that to give reality to this objective the government would have to develop the long talked about but totally ignored industrial strategy for Canada. Central to this would be development of a program for regaining Canadian control over Canadian industry. This is particularly important in the resource field where we must ensure that resources existing in Canada now and which are more frequently than not exported to the United States, Germany, Japan or some other industrial country, are kept at home for secondary manufacturing, processing and development. What I am saying is that an employment strategy that has as its objective the possibility of a job for every adult man and woman in Canada ultimately depends upon the restructuring of the economy and upon this government taking seriously the obligation of regaining control over our own economic destiny.
I have made some specific suggestions about what the government should do in the short run and in the long run. I say to the minister who is about to reply that we should have had a budget months ago to deal with our disastrous level of
Economic Policy
unemployment. I plead with him that when the budget comes down on March 31 it concerns itself with emphasis on job creation, that the proposals brought forward to create jobs will bear equitably on middle and low income people, and that it will be a first step to a long-run national commitment to permanent full employment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would apologize for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) who is absent today. He already had engagements in Washington and New York. He apologizes to the House for not taking part in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, inflation and job creation are not separate and self-contained problems. Responsible economic leadership has to take account of both problems at the same time. That is what the anti-inflation program is all about. The major goal of the government is to steer the economy on the path of stable and steady growth, not just for the next six months but for the future. We are a major trading nation; we have to sell abroad; we compete against imports in our own markets. We cannot adequately protect jobs or create new jobs for our growing labour force if our prices and costs are out of line.
The Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Callaghan, who leads a socialist government, recently remarked that governments cannot delude themselves into thinking that they can buy their way out of unemployment. Countries have to get their costs right. That is why that socialist government continues to grapple with an incomes policy and is forced to make massive cuts in public spending because the lesson has been learned too late.
This is increasingly understood by the major industrial countries. What we see in the world today is a careful balancing of the inflation and unemployment problems, a careful management of the recovery from the slowdown of 1974-75. Of course, this will require adjustments to be made to keep the balance. I will refer later to steps we have already taken. The Minister of Finance will decide what further steps are necessary in preparing his March 31 budget.
On the inflation front we have made a lot of important progress. We have had the increasing support of the country. We have also had the support of the provinces, including the New Democratic Party governments who have to live with the facts of life and the responsibilities of government. In fact, it is such a successful program that the last few weeks have shown that many Canadians do not want to see an early end to controls.
The government's view is well known. If we can get agreement about responsible behaviour in terms of wages and prices, then we can do without mandatory controls. That is the issue. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said, controls are a breathing space where we have to sort out, together, what is reasonable and responsible. We are working very hard at that process with business, with labour and with the provinces, and we are making good progress.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even if I take the place of my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), 1 would like to use these few minutes to comment on the situation of our economy and on the steps which are taken within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to stimulate the Canadian economy.
Concerning export programs, every day in the House I answer questions showing that Canadian products are making an ever wider breach into export markets. As far as the province of Ontario is concerned, for example, again this week I heard representations from contractors who are going to present very soon to Venezuela an important plan to get the contract for the equipment and the electric controls related to the construction of a subway in Caracas. A few weeks ago Ontarian contractors were awarded two of the three contracts for the construction of the Caracas subway.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I visited Venezuela myself and, in cooperation with a group of Canadians representing industries from Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario and Alberta, we made a proposal for the construction of a 700 kilometer railroad from Caracas to a western province in Venezuela, to introduce Canadian technology in that country. We made such considerable progress that we submitted the lowest tender. We expect to be invited soon to negotiate a contract with the government of Venezuela to carry out a part of this project.
I also want to answer the hon. member from Ontario who made representations as to how we stimulate employment in industry. I would like to tell him that only a few weeks ago, in Toronto, I gave supplementary credits to de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited to help convert the DASH-7-the STOL aircraft-into a patrol aircraft. I think the future looms great for this aircraft. Why? With the Canadian technology in this area, we are going to hit the market at the right time and this aircraft is going to consume much less fuel over fairly short distances than those jets we are using now. It is a short take-off and landing aircraft which I hope will make it possible to develop downtown to downtown services. We are now working in cooperation with the Department of Transport to implement a DASH-7 service between downtown Montreal and downtown Toronto and perhaps Ottawa. This aircraft is so advanced as regards elimination of noise pollution that it is not more noisy than a bus on a freeway, which means that the level of noise during take-off and landing is not essentially higher than that made by a bus. For instance, if one day we were to use the downtown Toronto airport on the island, the people on shore would not be aware of any take-off or landing. It is not more noisy than a Cessna, maybe even less. This is a Canadian technology which we want to promote and I intend to exhibit the DASH-7 during the Paris air show next summer and to travel in the near future to Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. I have asked de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited to send the plane over there so that I can use it to show it to the authorities there because I believe Canadian technology can be very useful on markets which are presently developing.
Economic Policy
People wonder what I am doing. Someone in the House said earlier: Tell us what you are doing to protect the textile or footwear industry. Everybody knows that we have moved very diligently in this regard. Two months or so after taking over the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, we have imposed quotas on all imports because we felt we had allowed too many imports and that we were or would be losing a substantial number of jobs. Now, no later than today, I talked to the president of a large Canadian textile and clothing firm who said that the policy I have put forward about two months ago in this field had already resulted in increased orders.
I could go on like this, Mr. Speaker, in many other fields. However, I might talk for a few seconds, with your permission, about the famous LearStar jet project. I was asked questions in the House this afternoon on that matter. This is becoming one of the greatest success stories in the history of industrial development in Canada. Within three months, we have already sold 71 aircraft at a cost of some $5 million each. The prototype is not even completed but a combination of factors, the fact that it is a long-range plane with a range of over 5,000 miles and a fuel consumption of approximately two thirds that of competitive aircraft, the fact that the demand is greater for that type of plane since many air services have been discontinued throughout the world and executives feel the need to buy planes for their business trips, and also that we now have the expertise in Canada to build that plane, for all these reasons it is a very exciting program.
Today, less than six months after Canadair first became interested in that project, 60 orders with deposits have been placed and contracts signed. The tunnel testing is giving better results than expected.
I am informed that the sales committee set up by Canadair will probably result in the following situation: by the end of 1977, a total of 131 aircraft will have been sold, the minimum required for that project to be completely profitable. I only want to give you one example. By the end of this year, as I have just said:
We shall probably have 131 planes, the minimum number required to make the project viable. Just to show you, Mr. Speaker how these things work, I can tell you that when de Havilland developed the famous Twin Otter they had made 20 before they sold one; and the Twin Otter program has resulted so far in the sale of 540 planes. Compare that with the LearStar program. The success is unbelievable. At this stage, when we do not even have a prototype flying jet, we have already sold 79, and by the end of the year sales may well have reached the 100 mark.
So here in Canada, with the help of Mr. Lear, the engineering genius from the United States, we have been able to develop a concept which is extremely attractive and which puts Canada in the forefront of this high-technology industry around the world. I might add that of the 79 sales made so far, only two or three are for the domestic market. All the others

are for export. So we have a great advantage. This project is creating jobs in Canada and the high-quality finished product is being sold around the world. This is one example of the job of work the government is doing in an effort to maintain our capability in the field of high technology while increasing our exports abroad.
I could speak of many other things. The debate this afternoon is very welcome on the part of those who sit on the government side. My colleague, the Minister of Finance, will be presenting his budget within three weeks and 1 hope every member who takes part in the debate today will make a concrete proposal. Here is an opportunity for them to express their views. I have been assured by my colleagues that their suggestions will be carefully looked into. Of course, not all the suggestions we make-and here I include my own-are accepted in the decision-making process. But all of them will be considered by my colleague in the preparation of the budget.
In conclusion, may I say that of course we face many problems in Canada. Unemployment exists side by side with inflation. The leader of the New Democratic Party mentioned the situation in West Germany. I would make it clear to him that, like any other country, it is our desire to see full employment and I will never stop working toward that end as long as one man wants a job and is unable to find one. But it is not possible to compare the situation here with the situation in West Germany. In Canada since the war the labour force has increased by 150 per cent, while in West Germany there has been virtually no increase in the labour force. West Germany imports labour from Italy, Spain, Portugal, and so on. When there is a recession, those workers go back to their country of origin. This is not what we do in Canada. When an immigrant comes here he has an opportunity to settle permanently. We have welcomed a lot of immigrants to Canada.
We want to find a proper solution to our difficulties, but 1 would point out that some of our problems today are due to the success of the economic policies of the government in 1974 and 1975, for example. For 27 months the Americans were in a deep recession. Here in Canada there was not much growth, but there was some growth-.6 per cent in the first year I mentioned and almost 2 per cent in the following year. Last year it was 4.6 per cent. So it is difficult for us to show the same numbers as the Americans because of the catch-up on the American side. We had less to catch-up with than they did.
For the first time in the economic history of this country we find ourselves with less unemployment than the United States, despite the fact that winter conditions south of the border are altogether different from ours-though admittedly the difference has not been so marked in the winter we have just experienced. But in the last three years unemployment in Canada has been less than in the United States. When one realizes how closely the two economies are intertwined, it must be admitted we have done rather well.

Well, I said a few moments ago that I would not stop working to create employment opportunities while there is one person in Canada who was looking for a job. In Canada we have tried to cope with some of these questions through job-creation programs. We have probably one of the most generous programs to alleviate unemployment that there is. Some critics of the government claim at times that our social and unemployment programs are so generous that a percentage of Canadians refuse to work because they feel happy with the level of support given by the government. I am just telling the House that we have done better than the United States, but we are not satisfied with the situation. We want to keep people working. The budget of the Minister of Finance at the end of the month will be another step in this direction.
May I say in closing that despite all of the problems we have in this country, I would not trade my nation for any other nation in the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say I accept the minister's last statement unreservedly. 1 want to place some comments on record for the edification of my colleagues on the other side. First of all, I charge this government, notwithstanding what the minister has just said, with foot-dragging, procrastination and with callous disregard for the plight of the one million people who are unemployed, as well as for those who may soon join the same line. A budget is long overdue. It is inexcusable that we must wait until March 31. After all the hollering and screaming and concern which has been registered for months now, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) comes kicking and screaming and has now decided to give us a date.
Having said that, I suggest that in framing a budget the following priorities should be considered; a reduction in unemployment, with the emphasis on the private sector; an improvement in terms of return on investment and capital expenditures; a re-emphasis placed on the market system; an improvement in the competitive position of Canadian industry; an improvement in productivity, in business and in labour confidence; and an unwinding of controls-the last of which, in my view, is of extreme importance.
As has been stated by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance and the chairman of the AIB controls have, in effect, adversely affected investment, productivity, employment, business confidence, initiative and labour problems. In his statement before the federal-provincial conference on February 1 the Minister of Finance gave five reasons why the green light was on for decontrols. I want to put them on the record. He said in his speech:
First, the economic situation throughout 1977 and into 1978 looks relatively favourable for exit from the controls program . . . Consequently, the economic situation would appear to give us a green light for decontrol.
The second factor that must be considered is the state of expectations. It gives us a more ambiguous signal. . . The decline in inflationary expectations stems from the better price performance recently experienced, and the commitment of most of our governments to the anti-inflation program . . .
March 8, 1977

The third factor is business confidence. Corporations are finding the prices and profits regulations administered by the AIB to be burdensome, and there is cause for concern that firms may be holding back on new investment projects .. . But the existence of controls, and in particular, the apprehension that they may remain in effect for a long time, is an added handicap . . .
Fourth, a significant benefit which can be derived from the development of an orderly program for decontrol and the necessary post-control arrangements can be a renewed basis for constructive co-operation with organized labour. One aspect would be renewed participation by labour in the work of important boards and councils.
I suggest that needs no explanation. Then the Minister of Finance said:
Fifth, I should note the problems that will crop up as the expiry date of the legislation nears. As the anti-inflation program moves into its third year and as its expiry date comes closer, the enforcement of controls will become increasingly difficult.
Those statements of the minister need no further elaboration. I need only re-emphasize that we will be moving a motion around March 31 to the effect that controls should end. The date for this remains to be seen.
If I may deal specifically with the budget, I should like to put some points on record. My party would like to see in the budget the following provisions: first, recognition that permanent employment is created not by government programs but, rather, by strong economic expansion in the private sector; second, stimulation of the housing industry in terms of construction of homes which people can afford, and 1 underscore the words "which people can afford"; third, tax cuts for middle and low income earners, thus encouraging consumer spending. We have long called for such a policy.
Fourth, the introduction of special fiscal contracts with companies wanting to locate or lease new industries in underdeveloped areas; fifth, encouragement in the areas of research and development in order to protect the future; sixth, a definitive statement on decontrol and post-controls, thereby regaining the confidence of both labour and management; seventh, economic forecasts and targets dealing with growth, job creation, inflation, unemployment and government spending both in the short term and in the long term. By long term 1 mean about two to three years. It is absolutely ridiculous that at no time can we challenge this government's forecasts and targets except on a year to year basis. We want to see what the government is doing and how it is proceeding. Then last, but certainly not least, we want to see the government honour its 1974 election promises regarding urban transit which in effect would have conserved energy and created employment.
On reading the motion 1 am reminded of my leader's speech of February 10 on a motion that we put forward condemning the government's complacency in the face of economic stagnation. My leader expressed concern about the sense of stagnation that exists, blaming the government, as did others-and rightly so-for the stagnation caused by the government's refusal to give any priority to the need to stimulate economic growth and to generate jobs. He pointed out in no uncertain terms and with great emphasis, as reported at page 2924 of Hansard:
We have been stagnant too long. We have a country to build. We have jobs to encourage. We have great promise to achieve. It will not be done by the timid
Economic Policy
policies of this government. It will only be done if there is determination to realize the potential of this country.
The Globe and Mail, as far back as November 4, 1976, in its lead editorial painted a very vivid but very sorry picture as a result of the findings of the university of Toronto's Institute for Policy Analysis. I quote from its lead editorial headed "More jobless unless Ottawa acts":
If the federal government doesn't act quickly to stimulate new business activity and new consumer spending, unemployment will get even worse than it is now. There will be 868,000 Canadians out of work the year after next-nearly
200.000	more added to the existing host of unemployed in this country.
That's the alarming prospect held out in a study released this week by the
University of Toronto's Institute for Policy Analysis. It says Canada faces continued sluggish growth and even higher unemployment for the next few years "unless the government acts to revive the flagging private domestic sector".
The last paragraph of this lead editorial reads:
Timing is everything. And the time for a budget to provide the necessary nudge-a hearty shove, even-to the Canadian economy is now.
That was written on November 4, 1976, but could well apply to the budget to be brought in on March 31, 1977.
What does the NDP motion mean? It implies we are spending $4 billion on unemployment insurance, and rightly so. I say that in the sense that no one wants to be without income; yet no one wants to be unemployed or on welfare. But the unemployment rate is the result of this government's attitudes, of its bankrupt policies and programs which were a disincentive to work. As the NDP leader said, we are losing billions of dollars in lost productivity and millions of dollars in taxes, and high unemployment is contributing to national disunity.
I do not have time to deal with these points, but they are a fact. Thinking Canadians agree that large-scale unemployment is an indefensible waste of our most important resource-our human resource. Although the motion has merit, and I pat my NDP friends on the back, it lacks one vital ingredient. It does not say that the budget should reflect faith and support for private enterprise which can create jobs. When you mention private enterprise to my friends on my left they reply with a tirade of abuse, refusing to accept the much desired and effective role of private enterprise.
What is the reality? Mr. Speaker, permanent employment is not created by government programs; it is created by strong economic expansion in the private sector. As we look ahead to the balance of 1977 we must spare at least a moment to look at the year behind us. Most of us would say that it is thankfully behind us. If one stretched one's memory back to last spring one could recall prophecies saying the economy was pulling out of the 1975 recession and increased exports would sustain a Canadian economic boom in 1976 and 1977. The Minister of Finance foretold a growth rate of 5 per cent in 1976 and
250.000	new jobs for the unemployed. Things, however, did not work out.
We now know that the budget forecast missed the mark. I hope any forecasts the minister will make in his budget address on March 31 will not be as wide of the mark as the forecasts

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
he made on May 25. Facing the mounting evidence provided by private sector economists, the minister conceded that the economy would not achieve its 5 per cent growth target. As for job creation, it appears that less than 85 per cent of the expected new jobs will materialize. Also, the unemployment rate, instead of holding steady, is slowly rising.
Although 1976 was a bad year, it may appear good by comparison with 1977. Even the Minister of Finance has shed some of his Micawber tendencies and admitted economic growth in 1977 is likely to be lower than in 1976. Economic and fiscal physicians, if I may call them that, warned the minister this would happen; unfortunately, he disregarded their advice. How much lower our economic growth will be is open to question. At least two internationally respected forecasting organizations predict that our economy will grow between 3 per cent and 3.5 per cent.
Forecasters indicate that job creation will proceed at an even lower pace in 1977 and the unemployment rate will continue a steady rise to more than 8 per cent by year end. The apparent presence of large amounts of slack in the economy will not create appreciable benefits in terms of price increases. Inflation rates may increase somewhat during 1977, rising to as much as 8 per cent. Both the OECD and the Conference Board suggest that the government's price target of 6 per cent for the second year of the anti-inflation program may not be achieved. This we understand; even the minister admitted as much.
Declines recorded for 1976 in the real value of business investment are likely to be repeated in 1977, and spending on new housing will contract after the 1976 boom. This anticipated decline in business investment in plant and equipment may be traced to a number of facts, including continued overcapacity, weak profits, uncompetitive exports, unhappiness with the government's mishandling of the economy, and uncertainty about the country's political future. The Conference Board forecasts that real business investment spending will decline by 2.5 per cent, or $670 million, in 1977.
Almost certainly this will not be a prosperous year for the one million unemployed, for those in disadvantaged regions where tens of thousands of people are condemned to chronic unemployment. It will not be a prosperous year for those leaving university, community college and high school, for their chance of finding a job is lower today than at any time since the 1930s. For them and many other Canadians 1977 will be a year of disillusionment, a year which may well leave lasting scars across our social landscape.
I resent very much the minister's relating our predicament to that of the United States and saying that things here are not too bad. How can you say that when one million of our people are out of work? They expect action. They expected it long before March 31. Canadians know from their direct experience that between 1967 and 1977 the Canadian economy performed poorly. They know that its performance during the period 1974 to 1977 was disastrous. But the government has taken no action. We hope it will do something meaningful on March 31. The Economic Council of Canada, the Conference
[Mr. Alexander.)
Board of Canada, the OECD and the University of Toronto Institute for Policy Analysis-all respected fiscal physicians- have noted the weak and depressed state of our economy and urged the need for stimulus.
1 read the editorial printed on November 4, 1976, and noted the financial position at that time. Noted authorities told us that we faced disaster, but the Minister of Finance remained silent, ignoring their advice. They told us about slow growth, higher unemployment, decline in business investment and decreasing export business. In the face of this, I submit the government should have brought down a minibudget to avert the danger of economic chaos. But no, that was beyond the comprehension of the Minister of Finance.
We need a new climate in this country, a climate of positive direction, of confidence in government policies, policies which unfortunately this government will not introduce. At present we are leaderless and rudderless. This condition reflects the government's bankruptcy and reflects our economic chaos. What has been the government's answer to date? Canada Works, Young Canada Works, and amendments to the UIC legislation. The government thinks it will save money by increasing the minimum work period from eight weeks to 12 weeks. Incidentally, where is that bill? First the government introduced it, then when Liberal backbenchers became nervous they did not proceed with it. I understand it is to come forward again. That is the government's "on again, off again" approach to this important legislation.
These programs are extremely unsatisfactory in their approach. It is an ad hoc, piecemeal process which makes mockery of a very serious matter. You are building up hopes and aspirations, but in the long run there is nothing lasting or meaningful in the types of jobs to which I have referred. Canadians need jobs. They demand that meaningful and lasting jobs be created. In my view, this can best be accomplished by the private sector through private enterprise. But what does the private sector say? I have here the pre-budget submission of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I have no hang-ups about the Chamber of Commerce. I believe they represent a very significant sector of the economy. This is what they said:
Business capital spending has been declining since the end of 1975, and the outlook is not encouraging. Business confidence is now at the lowest point in recent memory. The threat of aborted recovery, weak markets, a corporation tax structure that compounds the ravages of inflation, controls over wages and profits, and the stultifying effect of excessive government controls and regulations are all contributing to this serious deterioration in businessmen's confidence about the future environment for growth and development in Canada.
I believe that the health of our investment and capital markets is important for job creation and labour productivity.
