speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, 1 do not have much more to say, but let me put one more thing on the record. I hope my colleagues will not mind because it may take two or three minutes to read it, but I will do so as quickly as 1 can. It regards manufacturing. My friend to my left has indicated, as I do now, that manufacturing is in serious trouble. Canada's balance of trade in end products of the major commodity groups is in a serious deficit position, in the billions of dollars, which is affecting about 250,000 jobs. We know that the chemistry industry is operating at 83 per cent of its productive capacity, the electrical products industry at 81 per cent of its productive capacity, and the durable goods industry at 82 per cent of its productive capacity.
Let me put on the record what the president of Westing-house wrote to me, and I think to many hon. members. It registers his concern about the future of the electrical manufacturing industry in relation to GATT negotiations. He wrote:
We are the only industrialized country where provincial policies inhibit the national development of a secondary manufacturing industry that can be internationally competitive. Some provinces actively seek imports, others, in the thrust for industrial development, encourage further fragmentation of industry.
These circumstances cause two undesirable results. First, our markets are exposed to easy penetration by foreign manufacturers and, second, the relatively small and fragmented Canadian market cannot provide a sufficient base to make Canadian manufacturers internationally cost competitive.
The Canadian manufacturer pays the highest wages in the world, he pays relatively more for transportation due to the geographic distribution of the population, and despite the abundance of natural resources in this country he now pays world prices for raw materials.
In my view, the federal government has been most reluctant to address these problems, and, in fact, has aggravated them with its emphasis on broad international freer trade policies over the past decade. Pursuit of these policies has resulted in a worsening trade balance in every group of manufactured products and with all our major trading partners. The net result has been fewer jobs, lower investment and reduced output.
While this company supports liberal trade policies, it also believes that trade must be conducted fairly, without discrimination and with reciprocity. The realities of world trade in many electrical products are at variance with these principles. In every country where an electrical industry exists, actions have been taken to ensure its continuing viability as the technological backbone of those countries. Canada has taken no such action and, as a result, inroads have been made by foreign imports. Our trade deficit in electrical products has quadrupled over the last decade, taking an estimated 20,000 new jobs out of the country during that period.
There can be little question that in coming years Canada will have to rely to a greater extent on the goods producing sector in order to provide the job opportunities which will be demanded by the well educated new entrants into the labour force. For this to happen, we must recognize the need to preserve appropriate secondary manufacturing capability. It is wishful thinking that this country can accept a tariff cut in the order of 50 per cent on all its manufactured products without destroying much of the job-creating potential of this sector.
I want to thank hon. members for giving me extended time, thus enabling me to register my concern regarding the GATT discussions which will be taking place or are taking place. In conclusion, let me say that I hope, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) said, that the Minister of Finance will read the speeches made here today because I think-as a matter of fact, I know-that we in this opposition party have given him concrete suggestions. We have presented to him the priorities which he should be studying so as to adopt in his budget, if not all the proposals we have made, at least some of them so the we can provide long lasting and meaning-
Economic Policy
ful jobs not only for those who are presently unemployed, who now number some one million, but also for those who will join them unless a meaningful budget is brought down.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate on this opposition motion which was moved by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). This gives me the opportunity to follow up the excellent speech made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien). He has given us some background information on his strategy, but he has mainly dealt with the effects of the industrial strategy of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I was quite impressed by the success achieved by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in connection with the building of a subway in Caracas as well as a 700 kilometer railway line. If Canada is the lowest tender, this will no doubt mean more jobs for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I was also very proud to be a Canadian when I realized to what extent Canada was in the vanguard in the field of aeronautics and job creation in manufacturing through the contract awarded Canadair for the production of 71 Lear-Star jets. In my opinion, this announcement by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce shows that the government is well aware of the importance of developing an advance technology industry, namely the aeronautics industry, in order to create an increasing number of jobs by manufacturing more of those products in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal especially with paragraph 3 of the motion regarding urban transit. Today, I would have preferred that we proceeded with consideration of Bill C-33, the purpose of which is to define the objective of the transportation policy and to authorize the consequential rearrangement of powers, and so on. I would have preferred to go on with the second reading of Bill C-33 concerning the new objective of the transportation policy for Canada so that it could be referred to the committee for clause by clause consideration; this would allow us to implement as soon as possible this legislation on transportation which all Canadians have long been waiting for. And as the former transport minister said, if the Department of Transport is really a mess, we should at least have the opportunity to define once again the objective of the transportation policy for Canada. However, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate concerning urban transportation and the role of the federal government within this service.
The growth of urban communities as well as the increasing number and use of cars certainly represent a serious problem for all governments not only in Canada but in the whole world. The mover of this opposition motion condemns the government for its policy concerning urban transportation. In my opinion, he should have been much more specific or else he should have given a clearer definition of the urban transportation problem. He should have tried to better focus the problem, in order to

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
see, define and understand better so complex a problem as that of urban transport.
Public transport is closely related to the layout of cities. In some of them, up to 40 per cent of the land is set aside for transport. The problem therefore cannot be envisaged only in terms of those considerations and cannot be isolated from the other transportation systems: it should instead be integrated into them. To illustrate the extent to which public transit should be increasingly integrated, one need but study the situation that now exists in Montreal on the south shore and the north shore where it is essential to integrate public transportation.
In the light of that information, Mr. Speaker, one can conclude that rapid transit systems are primarily a provincial problem. Indeed, it is the responsibility of the provincial governments but, unfortunately, for too many years, provincial governments and cities have rather overlooked the problem, stressing private transport or the development of intracity expressways and throughways, or again intercity highways. Public transportation has been so neglected that today we have twice as much to do in order to provide Canadians with public transit that can at least compete with the other means of transportation. Provincial governments, and I insist on that, Mr. Speaker, have tended to show more interest in roads, superhighways for cars at the expense of public transit and other means of transportation, and that goes as well for cities as for the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the intervention of the federal government is justified because the provinces have given preference to public transport at the expense of public transport. We have not changed our minds and we still want to help the Canadians who must use a mode of transport in the evening or in the morning. All hon. members on this side of the House are aware of the importance of urban transit. Hon. members on this side of the House have certainly made the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) aware of this problem of public transport in the cities on many occasions, either at special meetings or at special caucuses.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members on this side also tried to influence the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in order to obtain more money for public transport. All of us entirely agree that this is a very important matter and that we must make every possible effort, and even superhuman effort to help upgrade public transport in the budgets, considering the monetary situation and this very important service.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, we should not believe that nothing has been done in the area of public transportation. I noted the speech that the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) delivered during the debate of March 3. If we were to consider every request made for money to be put in public transport, we would never see the end of it. The hon. member for York-Simcoe mentioned a budget of $200 million for the Toronto area alone. If we were to give the same or even more consideration to Montreal, the metropolitan region, we could not even set up a public transit system which we could rightfully expect. Therefore it goes without saying that

because of the inflationary situation priorities have to be established.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that we have done a great deal of things in that area. In cooperation with provinces and municipalities the government set up a development program, launched research work and granted a fiscal rebate of 12 per cent on bus purchases. For the province of Quebec alone this amounts to $35 million. For the City of Laval which also acquired buses it comes up to about $3 million. Then either through various methods, research, improved city planning or taxation, the federal government intervened to help the provinces and municipalities.
I should like to point out the implementation in Ontario, and more particularly in Toronto, of the GO-transit system which is now operated by the CN and whose costs are paid by the province of Ontario. The system is now working efficiently and I think that if the Montreal area is to benefit from an early solution to public transit difficulties experienced by CP on the south shore and by CN along the Lac des Deux-Montagnes from Montreal via Laval, the government of Quebec should consider the decision made by the Ontario government and apply an identical system which would be operated by the CN. Then I think that it would be an element of solution to the public transit issue and that could be done in the very near future. As of July 1, following an announcement by the CN the province of Quebec has to decide, after presenting its report on transit planning in the metropolitan area, what will be the future of the CN and CP in the Montreal area on the south shore as well as on the north shore. This is another way of helping municipalities and provinces provide local residents with better services.
At the beginning of my speech, I mentioned the growth of urban population. It is expected that, by the year 2000, 55 towns will have a population of 50,000 and that 23 of them are in Ontario and 13 in the province of Quebec. In other words, of the 55 towns which are expected to have 50,000 people in the year 2000, at least 21, representing a total population of 14 million, can be considered as part of a 700 mile long corridor stretching from Quebec city to Windsor. This will be a residential corridor, which brings me to say a few words about a newly established company, called Via Rail Canada. This CN subsidiary, which will be a management firm for passengers' services, will be responsible for the planning, marketing and provision of better passenger train services, within this Que-bec-Windsor corridor, which accounted last year for a potential number of 4 million passengers. An improved system will result in more milage per dollar and better accommodations for passengers, and, revised timetables will ensure a much more effective passenger service.
Mr. Speaker, I think I am not telling any member anything new when I say that CN and CP passenger rail services never were a business or an asset for those companies if one considers that passenger service last year represented only 3 per cent of CP's business figure and only 8 per cent of CN's and both CN and CP were piling up deficits year in and year out. In 1974, a deficit of about $25 million was recorded by those two
March 8, 1977

companies. Last year their combined deficit was about $32 million and following an amendment to the Railway Act in 1967 the federal government has been paying 80 per cent of both CN and CP liabilities from passenger service.
Consider that 80 per cent of liabilities are underwritten by the federal government. That amount last year was near $175 million, and it is estimated that unless changes are brought to the present situation a deficit of about $400 million will be recorded in the 1980's. Mr. Speaker, things should be made clear. The purpose of that CN subsidiary-Via Rail Canada- is not to compete with bus transport but rather provide passengers with a more adequate, much more comfortable service. That does not take anything away at all in terms of legal liability vis-a-vis CN and CP passengers. The formation of Via Rail Canada will bring about changes. We want to assure unions and employees that a program was developed whose main purpose is to provide a permanent job to those affected by the changes made in the railway passenger service system. Now we have assured those railway employees that a structure is now being set up to enable those CN and CP employees to find employment.
I wanted to indicate briefly how much we wish to improve transport conditions in municipalities as well as passenger trains. I want to assure all members in the House and the Canadian people that government members are so much aware of the importance of public transportation that we will have to obtain more funds. We are also aware of the fact that the government must make a choice and this is why we hope that the fight is not yet over, that it will still be possible to obtain additional funds for urban transit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on the motion of the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) which reads:
-That this House condemns the failure of the government to provide economic leadership and in particular its failure to introduce measures which will ensure economic growth and provide jobs for the more than 1,000,000 Canadians who need them; and calls upon the government, in its March 31st budget, to correct these failures by:
1.	establishing new direct job creating programs in needed social fields such as housing;
2.	reducing taxes for middle and low income earners; and
3.	assisting urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projects including rapid transit.
I think this is a true statement and that all members of the House view with alarm the staggering number of our citizens who are unemployed. The government figures show somewhere around 900,000; however, the leader of the New Democratic Party is no doubt much closer to the correct figure when he states one million, if we include those no longer registered for employment or eligible to receive benefits. Many people have probably given up all hope of securing a job through the Manpower office.
Economic Policy
In my riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka it is taken as a matter of course that a great many men and women find it difficult, indeed almost impossible, to secure year-round employment. A great many used to be engaged in the lumbering business and during those years there was always a two or three-month period in the winter when lumber camps closed before the sawmills opened. This is no longer the main industry but, thank goodness, there are still some sawmills operating in the riding which provide employment in a great many cases for longer periods. There are small and large industries in the riding which provide some employment. The largest employs 200 people. That may not seem very large to giants of industry such as General Motors and Ford. During the winter months especially it is almost impossible for those out of work to get a job. A great many of our citizens are engaged in construction work and tourism, both highly seasonal occupations.
I just talked to the Manpower centre in the riding and was informed that at the end of February, 1977, 2,947 people were registered for employment. This compares to almost the same number in February, 1976, when it was 3,072. The figures cover Muskoka and the east part of the Parry Sound district. The Canada Manpower Centre in North Bay reports that at the end of January, 1977, there were 2,246 male and 1,506 female unemployed, for a total of 3,752. These figures cover North Bay, Sundridge, Nipissing, part of Parry Sound, part of Renfrew North and part of Timiskaming. The Parry Sound Manpower office reports 1,700 registered clients without employment.
The minister recognized the serious unemployment in my area and increased the amount available for LIP grants to $801,000, more than doubling the original amount. A further $192,000 has been approved for Canada Winter Works programs, and $72,000 for the Young Canada Works programs. It was mentioned that a total of $200 million has be^n allocated for the LIP program. While this is certainly a large figure, it is still providing jobs that are of a temporary nature.The money is certainly acceptable, but it is only a temporary or band-aid approach. When the programs are over, the persons involved are back on the unemployment rolls. I will admit that this usually happens in the spring; those temporarily employed on such programs during the winter months are for the most part able to find other work in the summer season.
To improve the economy of the area and of many other rural ridings across the country the solution is to assist them in attracting industry and to assist small business and industry already located there to expand. This can be done by providing funds for expansion and for working capital at better interest rates and over a longer period of time.
The opposition motion also recommends job-creation programs that include housing. The recent report of the Canadian Council of Social Development stated that one-third of all Canadians cannot afford decent housing because government aid programs are missing their targets. There must be an overhaul of Canada's housing policy at the three levels of government in order to provide more housing for those in the

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
lower income brackets. When 280,000 families in Canada pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing, 500,000 families pay more than 35 per cent, 820,000 pay more than 25 per cent, and when two-thirds of those Canadians in need of housing cannot afford to buy or rent a home without government subsidy, we have a problem of tremendous proportions. We must take decisive action now or face terrible and unparallelled problems later.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) stated that during 1976 there were 287,000 housing starts. The government are to be commended for that. However, the great majority of those housing starts were for people in the middle income bracket. Those in the low income bracket could not qualify. At the present time only public housing is really answering the need of low income earners. This group suggests a better deal for non-profit and co-operative groups through subsidies and tax breaks, and directing government subsidies almost exclusively toward families at the bottom end of the housing scale. The villain of the piece can also be traced to the high cost of land and mortgage rates of interest. In order to further reduce the high cost of home ownership, our party would allow the deductibility from personal income tax of mortage interest payments on the principal residence. I have recommended that the government should permit the write-off of property taxes on the principal residence to a maximum allowable limit of $500 from personal income tax. At the present time this is an unfair tax on tax.
Consideration should be given to a more flexible National Building Code to'allow for regional variations. We also feel, and have advocated, that the 5 per cent federal sales tax on building materials should be abolished. This past year the government provided grants for home owners who had insulated their homes. I believe the figure is $300 for those who do the job themselves, and $500 if the job is contracted out. It so happens that those grants apply in only two provinces, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. It may just be a coincidence, but those are the only two provinces in Canada which have Liberal governments. I can assure the government that there are a great many areas in Canada where the economy is just as slow, the home owners are just as hard up, and there is as great a need for that type of assistance respecting insulation. I hope the government, in its wisdom, will see fit to extend this program. In my area of Parry Sound-Muskoka, and throughout northern Ontario, the climate is very extreme and insulation is very necessary. With insulation there would be considerable fuel saving.
It has already been pointed out that it costs 25 per cent more to live in Canada than it does in the United States. This applies to the cost of shelter. I think we can add another 25 per cent to the cost of living in certain northern areas of Canada. In the northern part of my province everything costs more. The people must pay extra costs over those paid in southern Ontario and other southern regions of Canada.
[Mr. Darling.)
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has finally announced his long-awaited budget for March 31. Let us hope that it will provide a reduction in taxes for middle and low income earners as requested in the motion we are debating today. It is absolutely necessary that the minister should come up with solutions and assistance to get people back to work on a continuing basis rather than the present hit and miss methods.
The leader of the New Democratic Party outlined certain credits at various tax levels. That is certainly food for thought and he is to be commended for it. Many urban communities, both large and small, are in dire need of financial assistance in order to proceed with necessary capital works projects. In Ontario alone, over 300 community arenas have been condemned as being unsafe. Federal assistance in this field would mean that many of these projects could be started immediately. The Ontario government has provided substantial and generous grants for these projects. However, many municipalities are finding it impossible to raise the balance through direct municipal taxation and private donations. Many towns and cities have building programs which are held up because of lack of funds.
It was suggested that the capital works program be reinstated. That is an excellent idea. I hope the Minister of Finance gives serious consideration to that suggestion. It was stated that at present there are 145,000 construction workers unemployed and receiving unemployment insurance benefits. I would assume that they are receiving the maximum benefit. If they were taken off the UIC rolls and put to work on these various building projects, it would be an excellent solution.
Our larger cities are very concerned about the lack of public transit. Metropolitan areas are crying out for federal money for rapid transit expansion. The high cost of gasoline and automobiles is making it necessary for the average working man and woman to leave the car at home and use public forms of transit. As hon. members are aware, the government placed an extra ten-cent tax on gasoline, which has been a great hardship to people who must drive to work each day-in many cases a good number of miles. In my own area many people from the small towns and villages commute to large centres such as North Bay, Parry Sound, Huntsville, Bracebridge, and Gravenhurst. Some of them drive as much as 100 miles per day. They are not allowed any deductions from their income tax for this purpose. This is discriminating when we consider that a great many taxpayers can qualify for business expenses. I am thinking of salesmen, doctors and many other people in the business world. These people for the most part have incomes much higher than the ordinary workingman.
I think of the people in northern Ontario, the area with which I am most familiar. Miners in the Sudbury area live considerable distances from the mines, sometimes 20, 30 or 40 miles away. Consideration should certainly be given to them. This applies even more to workers in industries which do not pay the high wages of INCO and Falconbridge. The industries in northern Ontario are resource industries. It would certainly be helpful if the federal government would provide additional
March 8, 1977

grants through DREE, and possibly other programs, to set up additional industries there to provide permanent, good-paying jobs to those who are now seasonally employed and find it difficult to obtain permanent employment.
I have to repeat what 1 have been saying in a great many speeches on a subject that is very dear to my heart, small business. Small business provides more than half of all the jobs we have in Canada. If we are to make any meaningful effort to tackle the present level of high unemployment we will have to look to helping this segment of our economy. In our system, whether or not the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) likes it, private enterprise can come up with better solutions to the problem of unemployment than the government. We must recognize this fundamental difference between our system and those of socialist or communist countries. In countries where the government owns and controls the means of production, distribution and merchandising, it stands to reason that the government will be the largest employer in the country. It is this basic difference that makes the present government's make-work programs inefficient and unsatisfactory in the long haul.
The millions of dollars spent on LIP and Canada Works will give temporary relief to a few thousand people, but what is really needed are long-term, career-type jobs which will allow workers to plan their lives just as we plan our own lives. Our people have a right to expect this. The hundreds of millions of dollars spent on ad hoc, make-work programs might better be spent encouraging business and industry to expand. We could use some of the money to encourage new businesses to be established. We now have a minister responsible for small business. While I have great respect for the hon. member appointed to that portfolio, I have to wonder if he is being given the latitude and support he will need if he is to make a meaningful contribution to this important segment of the national economy.
I have waited with a great deal of hope and anticipation to see if we are going to have a small business administration such as that in the United States to assist people in starting up in business, with both financial and informational assistance. A small business administration would enable prospective business men and business women to assess market conditions with respect to their product or service. It would not be possible to assemble all of the information one would need to establish a business, including up to date information in depth on the marketability of a product or service, without going to considerable expense. This information should be available from a central government source. Such an agency should be authorized to make long-term, low interest loans to businesses to purchase equipment and stock, to finance expansion and modernization and to facilitate the amalgamation of similar enterprises to form conglomerates or chains. It would also make capital available to people who want to start up a business or purchase or buy into a business.
Economic Policy
This agency that I envisage would have responsibility to study the different types of forms, reports and other kinds of paperwork that is presently imposed on small business people. The cost in time and expense to small businesses today just to keep up with the paperwork demanded by the government is causing businesses to fail every day. We simply cannot allow this pig-headedness and stupidity to threaten such an important segment of our economy. Much of the paperwork demanded of small businesses results from lack of co-ordination between agencies in government concerned with financial and commercial matters. It has grown unchecked through the years, and a large part of it is redundant and uneconomic. In many cases it is totally useless.
The whole body of Canadian business law needs to be overhauled, just as we have recognized the necessity to overhaul our criminal and civil law. It is ridiculous to pile still more laws and regulations on the body of law that is already stifling small businesses in Canada, which is in fact choking many of them to death every week. There are already so many forces in the market today mitigating against the interests of Canadian businessmen and exporters that we should be thinking of ways to help, rather than to hinder, small businessmen. We are no longer competitive in world markets, or even the continental market, with respect to a great many Canadian products. If businesses are forced to restrict their production and marketing to the domestic market, one already saturated with cheap imports, then it is small wonder that more and more small businesses are going under and that fewer and fewer are being established.
The complex tax structure small businesses have to cope with requires that even the smallest of them deal more and more with tax lawyers and accountants, neither of which come cheaply. We must seek ways to ease the tax burden on small businesses. If they thrive, we will more than make it up in increased profit taxes and taxes from the firms' employees. We would get increased production and a better level of services. If, on the other hand, we force businesses to go under, we get more and more unemployment and we reduce our tax base. We have a choice and we have the resources, but we have to make a decision.
There are other forces besides big government which work against the interests of small businesses. Small businesses, by their very nature, are unfavorable. They are vulnerable to pressures from big business and from big unions. They can be placed in an unfavorable or non-competitive position by the actions of big corporations. While we do have anti-combines laws which prevent such things as price-fixing, there are many ways, some of them subtle and some not so subtle, in which small concerns can be placed in an unfair position. They must have some avenue of appeal against unfair competition and business practices.
Small businesses and small industries are vulnerable to pressures from big unions, even more so than the larger corporations. For instance, while a man like Joe Davidson seems able to subject the Canadian people and the postal workers themselves to great losses in services and money, into

March 8, 1977
Adjournment Motion
the millions of dollars, on the pretext that the Post Office is not bargaining in good faith, we can survive these losses. Not so the small business or industry. Over and over again we have seen that one prolonged strike is all it takes to destroy a small firm, along with all the jobs that it once provided. Here again, employers must be guaranteed the same rights as the big unions and they must be afforded the same protection as the unions. They must have assurance that they can withstand the pressures, threats and actions that often accompany what would be normal and reasonable negotiations.

Let us help the business and industrial communities to solve this problem for us. Short-term, make-work programs are necessary to some extent to ease the plight of those who are chronically unemployed. But we must also recognise that we allowed this situation to develop to its present state. Spending millions, or even billions of dollars of taxpayers' money will not provide a long-term, permanent solution to high unemployment, unless that money is put in the right place. Non-revenue projects cost twice as much as the original grant because once the money is gone, there is no return. We cannot afford to use this approach as the basis of the cure.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me this is a most appropriate time to be discussing such a motion as my hon. friend for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has put forward. 1 say this in light of the fact that many agencies around the country are of the opinion that something more precise needs to be done with regard to reducing the level of unemployment. I agree with the previous speaker that a figure of one million unemployed is probably much more realistic than the figure currently provided. Like him, 1 find there are many in my riding who, although unemployed, are not registered with the Manpower office for employment. In fact, I would estimate that one-third of the unemployed are not registered.
The simple reason is that there is no work in the area; secondly, they have been unemployed for a considerable period. Their only solution is to move, and this they cannot do because of marital commitments. So there is a large body of unemployed who are not registered and are not taken into consideration by Manpower when deciding on winter works projects, LIP grants, youth project and other projects.
One of the things we fail to realize is that the government is the only body which is responsible for creating employment. It is easy for the government to put people out of work, and this government has done its very best to co-operate with the United States to leave the North American pattern unchanged without embarking on projects of its own which might solve unemployment in this country. The government decided, really, that the United States economy would be on the upturn in the last part of 1976, and it waited for this. It jointed in programs with our southern neighbour, but we have found ourselves in a worse position than the United States. Unemployment in this country is at a catastrophic level.
The government did embark upon a program which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in 1974 would not work. He indicated why it would not work and referred to the pitfalls that had befallen others who tried to freeze wages. He now
March 8, 1977

finds he has been proven corrected and that he is an able prophet. The Conservatives are now saying that the Liberals spoke against controls, that they then implemented controls and now look at the mess we are in. So the Prime Minister really has the worst of both worlds. He predicted that this would happen and he has now been proven right. One effect of controls has been to control only wages and some salaries. They have not been applied uniformly. Controls did not affect prices. It is of interest to note that a worker today can pay up to 50 per cent of his income for housing. Housing has not been controlled.
Interest rates today are the responsibility of the government. I was stupid enough, as were others in the House as well, to agree with officials who. told us that if we took off the ceiling on interest rates of 6 per cent, where it had been for years, it would create competition among the banks. It was the old, free enterprise idea that if there was competition interest rates would go down. Well, they sure went down, Mr. Speaker! In fact, they doubled, and in some cases considerably more than doubled so far as housing is concerned.
We have done nothing about interest rates. It is true that Canada is now in a very odd position. We have improved nothing and we find the value of our dollar going down. Our ability to borrow in the markets of the world is less than it was even a year ago. It will be difficult for the federal government and for the provinces to borrow money, all because the Prime Minister said he was the only one in this country who could unite the country. He now has us at the stage where there is some doubt that this can be accomplished by anyone; certainly it cannot be accomplished by him. Other countries are reacting to the situation and this is having an effect on our dollar. The cost to us is going to be very heavy.
What has happened to costs in this country? The AIB did nothing about energy costs or about medical costs. Really, it has done nothing about food costs. In fact, it did not do anything about anything, except to control wages and salaries. In the process it made business, management and labour very dissatisfied and cautious about any type of expansion in this country. The only body that can do anything about this situation today appears to be the federal government.
The federal government must do at least two things which are almost impossible to accomplish. Firstly, it has to establish some stability in our nation. This cannot be done by a referendum, by taking on "the enemy", or by somebody saying, "I am the only one who can be the saviour". This will have to be done with a great deal of co-operation, openness and willingness to negotiate. This certainly has not been the long suit of the present government.
Secondly, the government must do something about unemployment. As the previous speaker said, we have developed a number of ad hoc programs, though the government did not participate in the development of some of these programs. We have provided a sum of money for individuals and organizations if they come up with some kind of scheme. Such a scheme will be financed at almost the minimum wage in order to provide work for those who cannot find any other kind of
Economic Policy
work. But this has not done anything for the country. It is a stopgap measure, the kind of thing that has not done anything for the people involved.
As a rich country five or six years ago with a fairly high standard of living it was all very well to tell our young people to do their thing and we would finance it. But we can no longer enjoy that luxury. If we are merely supplying money today to provide minimum wages for people who in other instances would be on unemployment insurance or welfare, then we are not getting any great advantage and certainly there is no long-term benefit to the country. I can remember back in the fifties and even in the forties we used to talk about a shelf of works, the kind of work programs which the federal government would design and implement. The provinces would also design and implement such programs. From the federal point of view we even said we would be willing to accept projects which were designed and initiated by the municipalities.
We have come a long way from the day when the federal government was capable of designing make-work projects in this country, or when the provinces were able to design employment programs which were of advantage to the country, which created work that eventually led to full-time employment. All we are doing today is providing hand-outs. If you check, Mr. Speaker, you will find that this year these hand-outs had a lead time of about two weeks, or not even two weeks in most areas, from the time applications were made available to when programs were instituted at the municipal level and winter work was provided. It is a lousy program, the kind that will not provide any permanency of employment in this country.
What can we do? Last week an industry in my area closed because of the fight between Levesque and Trudeau, and the implications of that fight were noted on the money markets of New York.

That company was affected by our country's difficulties. Now it is most difficult for that company to continue its operation. If the government wanted to help, it could have instructed Texas Gulf, the company controlled by Canadian Development Corporation, to look into that property to see if it can be operated successfully. The Japanese will buy our asbestos. I am pleased at the development in my area, especially since the company met Ontario's health standards for the industry. I want to see it continue in operation. But it can only stay in business if the federal government asks the Canada Development Corporation to take the company under its wing.
I suggest that CDC should also look into other companies in my area. I am thinking particularly of a large, modern sawmill built not long ago at Kirkland Lake and employing 200 people. The government sank quite a bit of money in this mill in the form of DREE grants. But it was stupid because it did not take an equity position in that company and others like it which had received DREE grants. Some of these companies go bankrupt; and although the government has pumped large sums into them it has no say about their operations because it was not smart enough to take equity positions in them. If it took an equity position, a government representative would sit on the board of directors. In this way the government could provide technical knowledge and access to funds to tide them over serious difficulties.
The previous speaker said that free enterprise can do things more efficiently than can Crown corporations. That is not so. We have helped almost every business which started in this country in the last four or five years; unfortunately we did not take an equity position in them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Even the people involved in these businesses are happy to have the federal government as a partner. Why, Mr. [Mr. Peters.)
Speaker? They know the government will make available to them management experts, sales experts, and experts at raising money. I am sure the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) agrees that most industries we start in northern Ontario lack capital. Pretty well every one of those businesses is under-capitalized. For example, take the forest products industry.
We have in my area one of the most up-to-date little plants in the country. It produces flakeboard which is plastic covered and made into cases for stereo components for RCA Victor in the United States. It has been able to compete successfully with other companies engaged in the electronics field. I estimate the value of that plant at $9 million; I also estimate the capitalization at less than $2 million, and I am ignoring borrowings. Businessmen know that if you are under-capitalized to that extent, you are operating on bank loans, and banks will not carry loans indefinitely. If there is a drop in the price of the product, or a change in your rate of return, you must put new capital into your business or secure a large increase for your current revolving fund. This is true of businesses in northern Ontario, and equally true of those in northern Quebec. One hears almost constantly of businesses in those areas going bankrupt. What is the reason? They lack capitalization.
As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka suggests, if we were to take the money we now put into make-work projects and apply it to the establishment of long-term industries in northern Ontario, we could create long-term employment for people now living from day to day, working short intervals, trying hard to work eight weeks in order to qualify for unemployment insurance.
We should enter fields others mentioned. I will not cover them in detail. Housing is a good example. Mr. Speaker, we do not need the kind of housing builders are building today. In Timmins, a mining town, there is a great surplus of housing, expensive housing which people working in the mines cannot afford.

Mr. Speaker, I will end on this note: we need to examine our housing. I was speaking of Timmins. Not long ago I talked to one of the main contractors in that community and one of the leading real estate agents. He said that there is surplus housing in the community, but it is mostly of one kind. It is expensive. It is expensive because he must raise money to put in the sewers, water, roads, and other ancillary services which go into a subdivision. Mr. Speaker, we should provide municipalities with long-term money for picking up real estate
March 8, 1977

in areas not now under development. We should allow our municipalities to do some of that basic development. The municipalities could buy land with money provided for long periods at low interest. The interest cost on land is reflected in the purchase price of a house. I suggest that high interest on land costs and on the cost of services people must pay are not doing any good to the cause of housing.
Houses built for our underhoused population in this country should be low cost. 1 am one of those who believes that houses can be built at a reasonable cost and sold to those who want to live in that type of housing, if only the government would give the necessary leadership by enabling the provision of mortgages at a low interest, and giving the kind of assistance that is necessary to allow for a rapid expansion of the housing industry, which would have a spin-off effect on the lumber industry, the plywood industry, and other industries providing furnishings for those houses. In my opinion this will result in a greater rate of employment.
I would like to go on to speak about urban transit which should be improved in the city of Ottawa. I have in my pocket bus tickets that are two years old. They cost me four for $1. Last year they were three for $1, and this year they are five for $2. That is how quickly costs for transit are going up. One waits for a bus for a long time, and then it costs you 50 cents if you have a drop fare. It is just as cheap to drive your own car, but is it cheap for the nation in the energy that is used? Is it cheap for the city which has to build a new lane on the expressway because cars clog it in the morning? Our priorities are not very good. The forthcoming budget will allow the government to redeem some of the mistakes it has made over the last few years, but I hope the government will take full advantage of the budget to increase employment.

The whole question of rapid transit is one about which all of us who represent urban areas must be concerned. In my opinion the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan), in his remarks on March 4 in this place, offered arguments which were very unconvincing. He spoke about the need for conservation, but he did not deal
Economic Policy
with what is, in my opinion, the very important contribution in the form of energy conservation which is implied in the support of public transit. He spoke about the need for restraint, which I fully support without question.
In the debate in which we are taking part now we are offering some advice to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in the matters that he might consider in his forthcoming budget. I sincerely hope that in considering the problem of energy, which the Minister of Finance must do, he will look at what must be done by way of encouragement of public transit and discouragement of the use of the private automobile and the unnecessary consumption of gasoline.
I do not know what are the costs in the budget of subsidizing gasoline or, shall we say, of maintaining a generally uniform price structure for gasoline from one coast to the other. My colleague, the hon. member for Laprairie, yesterday suggested in the House that they might be in the order of $800 million a year, but these must be very rough estimates. The sums of money are very large indeed, and what I and my colleagues are seeking, those of us who are speaking in support of urban transit, is a long-term view. We ask the government not to be penny wise and pound foolish, not to undertake policies that are for the day only and that, over a long period, will cost a good deal more in funds which could properly be spent on urban transit now.
I said that I did not intend to make a lengthy speech, but if I may, I should like to talk about what is happening in this city.
I noted that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) referred to the bus fare structure in metropolitan Ottawa. I was an alderman on the city council for a number of years and saw the growth of what was probably a typical Ottawa suburb.
I represented on city council an area without a single apartment building. In large sections of the city there were almost only three and four bedroom bungalows inhabited by people bringing up their families in the family formation years. This brought a tremendous burden on the school system and led to an overbuilding of elementary schools in my part of the city. It distorted many of the priorities that a logical planning sequence would have indicated. My colleague, the hon. member for Laprairie, documented this very convincingly and eloquently in his speech in the House.
At this stage we have still the opportunity of putting forward some logical priorities in the field of urban transit, knowing that this is the only way, over a longer period, in which we can have a rational energy conservation policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
I speak not only of the encouragement of urban transit-and I want to speak about the means which, I hope, will shortly be adopted by the government-but also of the discouragement of the private automobile. It is not an easy thing to be a member representing a constituency such as mine and to support a charge for parking by government employees in the central core of this city. This government instituted a charge for parking in the fall of 1974. I have had only one or two complaints about it. I expected a deluge of complaints, but

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
the people I represent know that there must be a deterrent to the use of private automobiles. They know that the parking spaces they use cost the taxpayers money. They know also that it is infinitely better in every way if we can develop a good transportation system as an alternative.
I ask that the government carry the thinking a little further. The charges for parking should not only be at the central core of the city. I attended a community association meeting in my constituency last week at which the people there asked that charges be imposed at Tunney's Pasture-which is not really a suburb but at one time was considered a suburb-because they know now that the overuse of the existing parking facilities in that area creates a blight, a community nuisance, and is an inefficient use of energy. It pollutes the air, and is wrong in every way. The same can be said about Parliament Hill.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that you would convey to others associated with you in that office the need for a policy of charging for the use of parking on Parliament Hill. I am ashamed as a member of parliament to park my car on the Hill free of charge. My constituents pay when they drive their cars to work and park in the central area of the city, and I hope there will be an initiative from Mr. Speaker's office to bring about a re-examination of the policy of free parking on Parliament Hill for a chosen group. The policy is wrong, it cannot be defended in principle, and I will be delighted to pay my share of the charges which, I am sure, would be only right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
I am glad to hear hon. members on the other side support this.
We have to live with the necessity for conserving energy. We have to live with the fact that we cannot go on with the balance of payments problem which energy will create for us to a much more serious extent every year. We have to set individual examples.
I had the privilege of serving as a member of the transit commission of this city for some time. I learned then what a sad state public transit technology was in. I went with other members to San Francisco where a major program involving hundreds of millions of dollars was being undertaken. Before making their decision they set up their own laboratories to test equipment. They were testing four types of direct current motors, and about three types of alternating current motors. The problem in technology was as basic as that.
The metro in metropolitan Montreal was a tremendous thing. It adopted a technology which is now generally considered to be obsolete. Rubber wheels were put on steel rails, and, so that that could be done, the stations had to be designed to use gravity braking. The city of Montreal is not in a position to convert that system to anything else now because it is locked in with it. However, had appropriate technology been used in this cold part of the continent we know so well, had there been leadership from the federal government and from provincial governments, and had there been research and testing projects,

the basic decisions could have been made with greater wisdom and knowledge.
On March 2 in this House my colleague, the hon. member for York East, outlined what is available by way of research and demonstration project assistance in Canada. This has been available since 1972-73. My colleague pointed out that over the first four fiscal years the great total of $1.25 million was paid out by way of federal grants for demonstration and research and for urban transit technology. I suggest that that is hardly something in which we can take a great deal of pride.
There are certain provisions under the National Transportation Act, but we are not debating that act at this point. I welcome what is being done, but it is grossly inadequate. There is an opportunity for us in Canada today to put our money where we have an urgent, crying priority, and to solve in a technological sense the problem of how to move people from city to city -commuter transit-and the problems of urban transit, moving people within cities. Canada can make a contribution with the knowledge, the skills and the technical capacity which are available to us. This could be of great assistance to us not only with regard to our domestic problem but also in developing export markets in other parts of the world.
During the course of the 1974 election campaign the party to which I belong made a very explicit promise in terms of the type of assistance which would be available. I believed in that promise. I believed it made a great deal of sense. It was a matter of very deep regret to me to learn recently that there are people in responsible positions who suggest that that promise cannot be honoured. I, for one, will do everything I can to urge the government and others in this place to support a policy of aid for urban transit as soon as it is possible to have such a policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
First of all, I would like to commend the New Democratic Party because they put forward a motion today which condemns the failure of the government to provide economic leadership and in particular its failure to introduce measures which will ensure economic growth and provide jobs for the more than one million Canadians who need them.
Mr. Speaker, today's motion calls upon the government to correct these failures in its March 31 budget through three specific measures which read as follows:
1.	establishing new direct job creating programs in needed social fields such as housing;
2.	reducing taxes for middle and how income earners; and
3.	assisting urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projets including rapid transit.
Mr. Speaker, these three specific measures proposed by the NDP are most interesting and we would be hard put to find one member in the House who stands against developing our own resources while providing useful jobs to unemployed citizens who are deprived of any lucrative occupation. It is evident that establishing new direct job creating programs in
March 8, 1977

needed social fields such as housing represent a very valuable objective for us. But the problem is what kind of response this proposal will get from the government? It will surely answer that it has no money, that it has not the financial means to set up such programs with the limited funds presently available.
The same kind of answer will be given to any proposed reduction of taxes for middle and low income earners. Mr. Speaker, everybody agrees on the principle of the matter. In our opinion, our colleagues of the NDP did not invent the suggestion contained in the motion they put forward today.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit members have been asking for the same thing since 1962 and always the government, which at the time was led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) answered that it could not reduce the income tax of people in the lower income bracket. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said before supper time, the socreds have been demanding since 1962 what is being proposed today by the New Democratic Party. The government at that time which was headed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would readily reply that it could not reduce income tax for low income earners for the same reason given by this government today, namely that they did not have any money. The same thing occurred, Mr. Speaker, under the Pearson government and it is still the same now with the Trudeau government which claims it has no money, and is unable to reduce the taxes of low income people.
As for the NDP third proposal, I am pleased to point out that the development of urban communities through federal funding of public works is a matter in which social crediters have been interested for a long time.
When we suggest that public works sponsored by municipalities and provinces be financed through interest-free loans by the Bank of Canada, we bring forward a concrete and efficient way of enabling urban communities to acquire essential services without going into debt for thousands of years. We also know, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of that debt accounts for more than half of the budget of some municipalities. How can a city acquire the necessary services when half or more of its funds go to pay the interest on its public debt? It is obviously impossible. The proposal of our friends of the New Democratic Party to press the federal government into spending considerable sums of money for municipalities is certainly not the ideal solution. As a matter of fact, the only result of that solution
Economic Policy
would be that the federal government, instead of municipalities, would go into debt.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Crediters propose that municipalities get loans without interest from the Bank of Canada for their development. The Bank of Canada is the financial institution which must be the servant of Canadians. If this bank would lend the necessary sums in the form of new credits guaranteed by all our resources, municipalities could get on with the establishment of the necessary services without having to go into debt and get crushed by the cost of servicing the debt only. For all useful purposes, Mr. Speaker, the three specific measures put forward today by the New Democratic Party will merely be pious wishes as long as the government will not have money enough to realize all those projects. The NDP itself, if it were in power, could not implement the measures it is putting forward today, and we would hear the leader of the NDP complain about the lack of funds.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there is no shortage of Canadians ready to work. There is no shortage of manpower. There is no shortage of skilled people. As we are all aware, we have the necessary engineers, architects, technicians to carry out all those ambitious projects which could make life easier for us both in our cities and rural areas, nor are we lacking materials, Mr. Speaker. We have steel, concrete, all the metals and raw materials required for the construction of rapid transit systems as advocated by our colleagues of the NDP. How come then, Mr. Speaker, there are so many idle hands in our beautiful and wealthy country? How come it is impossible to realize our main projects in the social sector? We always get the same answer: because there is no money. And our NDP friends do not even talk about this problem which is a basic one, the prime source of our present difficulties.
The measures proposed today tackle the symptoms, the obvious signs of the problem but they do not deal with its deep causes. We all recall the former leader of the Social Credit party of Canada, the late Real Caouette, who used to say that dealing with the appearances of the problem is like putting a band-aid on a wooden leg. As the former hon. member for Temiscamingue used to say so well, so long as we have not thoroughly revamped the economic and financial system we will continue to hear the governments say: That is a good idea but we don't have any money. What we are asking for, with our Social Credit economic reform, is simply that the monetary system reflect today's realities.
Everyone admits that it is not normal for the government to be paralyzed by a lack of money, while thousands of people would like nothing better than to go to work, creating services and goods of benefits to all Canadian citizens. Nor is it normal, Mr. Speaker, to see that, in spite of the fact that we have within reach the materials required to give the services asked for by municipalities and individuals, we are unable to act simply for lack of money. Yet, subway and railway services, to increase the speed of urban transports, are not built with dollars, but with such materials as steel, concrete, plastics

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
and metals, and of course, with competent people, engineers, architects and technicians. And do we have all that here in Canada? What are we waiting for to put the financial system in line with reality? As long as we live in a monetary system that does not take into account the physical realities of the modern era, we will face that problem, we will discuss motions that are wishing thinking, and we will hear governments claim we are short of money. If the New Democratic Party is not prepared to propose a thorough reform of the financial and monetary system, it could at least propose some measures that might make it not so easy for the government to give us the same answer: We are short of money.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit party of Canada, of which 1 have the honour to be a member, has always included within its programme a clause recommending lowering the age of voluntary retirement to 60. As a result, not only do we support lowering the retirement age, but we press for old age security pensions and benefits under Canada Pension Plan that are high enough to guarantee the aged a decent living. Is Canada economically and financially able to meet the requirements of the motion now before us? The GNP is maintained at a reasonable level in spite of the increasing number of unemployed. They might contribute to increase the gross national product if they could use their energy to increase our national production, which would enable us to achieve the goal set out in this motion.
Mr. Speaker, one may also wonder whether Canada can financially afford such expenditures. As far as I am concerned,
I think that budgetary cuts are certainly necessary, particularly in connection with the servicing of the national debt. During the present fiscal year, the Treasury Board has to pay $4 billion in interests on the national debt, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) refuses to say to whom these interests are being paid. One only has to refer to the answer recorded in Hansard for February 1, 1977, in reply to a question No. 1389 put by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert).
The hon. member for Bellechasse was then seeking information which should be made available to all Canadians with regard to the total of the national debt. Who are our creditors? Is it a long or a short-term debt? It seems that we are always seeking information which apparently is never available. Interest is being paid and we cannot even find out to whom. There is money owing, but to whom?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to all such motions which have been moved since 1962, the government had always pleaded the lack of money. How is it possible to lack money when we do not even know to whom we are paying interest and owe money?
One other thing, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the government should develop as many job-creating programs as possible, such as LIP and Canada at work. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, an attempt should be made to keep the administrative costs of these programs as low as possible, so that the largest amounts possible will be appropriated for that purpose.
(Mr. Caouelte.)
Obviously many municipalities were able to establish services like recreation centres and arenas through LIP projects and this year's Canada Works. A few weeks ago 1 had myself the opportunity to participate in the opening of the Barraute arena in my riding, and that was done thanks to the jobs created by local initiative projects. And it is also because of the wonderful work accomplished by the municipal council of that town which achieved something very important for the people of that municipality. So I strongly encourage the minister responsible for those job creation programs to make all possible efforts to increase the funds available so that many more good projects can be implemented.
I wish to underline the fact that municipalities are now in a very difficult situation. Their revenues from land taxes are not enough to cover their financial burden. The interest on their public debts seriously affects their budgets. Again this week, Mr. Speaker, I met members from the Val d'Or municipal council who had to beg the Minister for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to get credits to lighten the financial burden of their municipality through the financing of some services. Mr. Speaker, that is only one example of the difficult position of our municipalities throughout the country. It is clear that tailoring job creation programs to the priorities of our municipalities is a positive and efficient means to reduce their terrible burden.
Then I encourage this government to make every possible effort within the present monetary structure to give first priority to job creation programs to develop municipal services. Of course, it would be more interesting to see the government undertake a reform of the financial and monetary system but I think we cannot count too much on the present government to show leadership in that field. In view of the constant administrative blunders of this government, we are not too enthusiastic about seeing it launch into major reforms which would be beyond the competence of its members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to participate in this debate brought on by the NDP. 1 think that at this time it is worth reviewing the motion they have placed on the order paper.
That this House condemns the-failure of the government to provide economic leadership and in particular its failure to introduce measures which will ensure economic growth and provide jobs for the more than 1,000,000 Canadians who need them; and calls upon the government, in its March 31st budget, to correct these failures by:
1.	establishing new direct job creating programs in needed social fields such as housing;
2.	reducing taxes for middle and low income earners; and
3.	assisting urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projects including rapid transit.
One criticism that I should make is that the motion nowhere refers to the private sector. Business capital spending has been declining since the end of 1975 and the outlook is not encouraging. Business confidence is at the lowest point in recent memory. The threat of aborted recovery, weak markets, a tax structure which compounds the ravages of inflation, controls over wages and profits, and the stultifying effect of excessive government regulations are all contributing to this serious deterioration in business confidence about the future environment for growth and development in Canada. Unless capital formation is given every encouragement, workers will lose now through more unemployment and less productivity and they will lose in the future by being paid pensions of lower real value.
We are all aware that the private sector of the economy provides many jobs. Unless this area is stimulated we shall see unemployment levels rise even higher. My hon. friend from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) outlined the position of our party. As usual, he did a superb job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
In the past little while our party has received a certain amount of criticism for not advocating policy. All one has to do is read the speech by the hon. member for Hamilton West. He has done a superb job of outlining the areas in which we feel the government should act. One thing that puzzles me even more than the criticism we receive for not advocating policies is that the governing party does not receive any criticism for not having any policy itself.
I ask hon. members opposite to tell us their policy with regard to the one million people who are unemployed. All one has to do is look at the immigration bill presently before parliament. What the government wishes parliament to do is pass the legislation so that regulations can be enacted by order in council. It does not wish to tell parliament or the Canadian people what those regulations will be in advance of the passage of the legislation. This can only lead us to believe that the government has but one policy, a policy of doing nothing and of securing its re-election at the expense of the expectation of the Canadian people.
Economic Policy
Turning to the motion, I wish to deal first with item number one which speaks of the establishment of new, direct job creation programs in social fields such as housing. Housing is at a critical stage. My first suggestion would be that interest payments on mortgages be tax deductible. I am sure this idea would receive reports from both sides of the House. Members of my own party and members of the opposition parties with whom I have had conversations have told me they would support such a move. The budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) intends to bring down on March 31 is the means by which to implement the proposal. Let us hope that in the budget we shall see something along these lines.
The motion speaks about establishing new, direct job creation programs. Let us hope any such programs will be more effective than those we have seen in the past. The minister recently announced the Canada Works program. In my opinion this program is nothing but a pork barrel for the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: Shame!

speechtext: We see this when we calculate on a Canadawide basis the amounts received by Liberal constituencies as compared with the amounts received by Progressive Conservative constituencies and others.
