subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: Nonsense!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
All we have to do is look at two constituencies. First, the constituency of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in Vancouver East. It is to receive $514,000. Now look at the constituency represented by our party whip, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski). It will receive $100,000. I am sure the unemployment rate differential is not so great as to warrant five times the amount of money going to the constituency of the Minister of Justice. If that is not pork barrelling I do not know what is.
Some time ago I asked the minister responsible for this program if he could explain the procedure used-the funding formula. Do you know what the minister said to me, Mr. Speaker? I asked the minister this question well over a month ago and he has not yet seen fit to reply. He has said absolutely nothing.
To deal with the second part of the motion, reducing taxes for middle and low income earners, I believe that taxes must be reduced for these people. A reduction in taxes will increase consumer spending, which at this point is what Canada needs. Canada's economic opportunities are in grave danger of being sacrificed to the apparent political opportunism of the Liberal administration. The economic situation is critical. Only by an immediate tax cut and an end to controls can unacceptable unemployment be avoided and economic growth restored. By delaying the taking of these needed economic initiatives, the

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
Minister of Finance is depriving Canadians of potential jobs and of more secure prospects for defeating inflation, with the chance of real gain and wealth for all.
In postponing the removal of controls until 1978, when the minister himself admits that they could be removed now, he is adding to uncertainties about the economic future for both labour and business. If economic conditions are favourable to the ending of controls, there is little reason to prolong the dislocations which an extended controls program brings. Is it just a coincidence that the end of controls in 1978 will coincide with the year of a likely federal election?
Most economists agree that our economy urgently needs a tax cut to restore growth and to create jobs. Progressive Conservatives have argued for reduced taxes since May of last year, and the need is now critical. Instead of responding to economic conditions through a display of leadership, the minister was vague about the date of the budget until a few days ago. The fact is that it will take six to nine months before the effect of a tax cut begins to turn the economy around. To avert tragic levels of unemployment this fall, tax cuts should have occured this past fall. But the Minister of Finance did not have the foresight to make those cuts. Even if tl)ere is a stimulative budget on March 31, the good effects will not be felt until 1978. Meanwhile, according to the NDP's figures, some one million Canadians remain unemployed and the economy stagnant. Is it a coincidence, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has deliberately delayed the good economic news until an election year?
If I may deal with the third part of the motion, which refers to assisting urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projects, including rapid transit, during the 1974 election campaign the Liberal administration, when it was on the hustings, promised $290 million to municipalities for rapid transit. It is now reneging on its promise. I think it is imperative that there be this expenditure on rapid transit. Failure to implement this promise is causing disastrous effects on municipal planning in areas like Edmonton. Rapid transit would relieve congestion in large urban areas. It would stimulate jobs for the unemployed, and the long term saving effect in regard to energy consumption would be felt in such areas.
Again I ask, what is the Liberal government doing in this regard? Absolutely nothing. Now is the time to implement measures to ensure the availability of rapid transit. This administration promised aid to rapid transit in 1974 to the tune of some $290 million; to date this promise has not been kept. Had we in the Conservative party promised aid to rapid transit in that amount during the 1974 election campaign I am sure it would have soon been implemented. It appears to me that this administration is inclined to flip flop frequently. All one needs to do is to look at what members opposite said about wage and price controls which we proposed during the 1974 election campaign. They stated that they would not work. We were condemned by our Liberal opponents.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: They were less than honest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: They were right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
In 1972 exactly the same thing happened. In that campaign we said we would index personal income taxes. We proposed modest increases for pensioners. Hon. members opposite did not like the idea of a modest increase for pensioners, yet immediately after forming a minority government they implemented what they had been campaigning against. And hon. members opposite wonder why we in the Conservative party are careful about bringing forward our policies. We want to make sure that if our policy is going to be stolen by the present administration it is correctly introduced, so that what the government brings in for the Canadian people is on the right scale.
Another suggestion of mine would be removal of capital gains tax on the farming population. This is one of the few ways in which individuals in rural areas can save for the future. So many of our farming population continue to invest while earning their livelihoods, and when they retire their only source of income is the revenue they receive from the sale of their land.
This capital gains tax also causes difficulties for them in other ways. If a farmer in my area were to sell a piece of property, he would have to pay capital gains tax even in the event that he reinvested in another piece of property. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Finance will take this proposal under serious consideration, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) said he would when he spoke in this debate on behalf of his colleague.
Another area I wish briefly to cover is the mail carrier service in Canada today. I am extremely pleased that within the constituency of Pembina there is the only area in all of Canada where the freeze on mail carriers was broken. For this I have to thank the then postmaster general, Bryce Mackasey, who gave us an additional five mail carriers for the residents of Mill Woods. There are other areas in Edmonton which deserve to have what Treasury Board term an essential service. All residents of Canada pay the same taxes according to their incomes, yet they do not receive the same services if they do not have available to them mail carrier service. As I said earlier, mail carrier service is termed an essential service by Treasury Board, yet this administration has seen fit to discriminate against a certain segment of our society in this regard. Let us hope that in the coming budget the Minister of Finance and the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) will make funds available to service all areas equally with mail carriers.
It is also interesting to note my good friend from Edmonton Centre recently sent out a questionnaire to his constituents asking them to share with him their various problems. On practically every second questionnaire returned there was a complaint having to do with the post office. It is interesting to note that the United States runs its post office department in co-operation with the private sector, and their budget has shown a surplus. The NDP, which is so socialistic, should investigate this area, because since the United States has involved the private sector in the operation of its post office,
March 8, 1977

the post office budget of that country has run at a surplus. Previously it had run at a deficit.
I hope the government will give high priority to legislation dealing with budgetary matters. The delay in enacting the May, 1976, budgetary proposals and the 10 per cent surtax announced in December, 1975, caused great uncertainty among taxpayers. Many taxpayers were forced to make decisions before the end,of 1976 on the basis of draft legislation which might have been amended before it became law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the hon. member who just resumed his seat did not want more time to speak. I see him shaking his head.
Economic Policy
I enter the debate this evening willingly, to speak on my party's most important motion. It deals with the economic condition of this country and the suffering of our people, suffering brought about because the government has failed to direct the economy adequately. I do not know if I will live long enough to see either a Conservative or Liberal administration in this country plan the economy. Those administrations seem to operate more or less on an ad hoc, day-to-day crisis basis.
When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) spoke this afternoon on my party's motion he went to great lengths pointing out the accomplishments of his government in recent years. The minister is to be congratulated for being able to paint a rosy picture at this time in our economic history when unemployment is higher than it has been at any time since Statistics Canada began compiling unemployment data. If I am not mistaken, more people are unemployed today than were unemployed in the 1930's. All this reminds me of John Steinbeck's "The Grapes of Wrath", only we have no California valleys to which our unemployed can trek in search of work. The government forces them to trek to unemployment insurance offices, to line up, sometimes to complain they are not getting their cheques, although through no fault of their own they are out of work.
The government's record in recent years in providing economic leadership has been totally abysmal. The rate of inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, remains unchanged when the food component over which the AIB has little control is excluded. Today Canadians find themselves basically in the same economic circumstances they were in before the imposition of controls. Really, the only accomplishment of which the government can boast is that, since October, 1975, it has distorted collective bargaining and penalized unfairly some of the organized and most of the unorganized working people of Canada. That is about all it can boast about.
The New Democratic Party suggested as far back as the last budget that the swelling unemployment rate was a major problem to which the government should address itself. The leader of my party stressed in speeches across the country that it is time to quit viewing unemployment as just a statistical problem and to begin dealing with it in human terms. This government simply doesn't understand the misery caused to the one million currently without jobs or under-employed, in the sense that they can only work part-time, perhaps one or two days a week.
The government thinks that by having unemployed workers receive an average of $96 per week from unemployment insurance the problem becomes less serious. The payment is a palliative. If the French monarchy had introduced a program like this in 1789, perhaps it could have averted the revolution. The program is a palliative; it allows people to subsist, and takes away the urge to go to the barricades and tear down our buildings.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is more interested in spending his time figuring whether 889,000 people are out of jobs, or if the figure really is 1,100,000. But he and his colleagues miss the point, that mentioning

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
various figures will not alleviate the plight of people out of work.

speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has now said that he will bring down a budget at the end of this month. Although I do not know what the budget will include, I can say one thing. Certainly no budgetary measures to be introduced on March 31 will have any effect on people now unemployed. As the Minister of Finance well knows, budgetary measures can take between six months and one year to have impact on the economy. That means that we could wait for the spring of 1978 to see a downturn in unemployment rates. Of course what will happen depends on specific measures announced in the March 31 budget, but judging from past experience it is safe to conclude that not much can be expected from this government. It is always a few months late. It starts planning in March to relieve winter unemployment. Really, it just makes no sense. Its actions escape logic. The government has consistently paid lip service to creating jobs for Canadians; as we have seen, its achievements to date have been nil.
I will recall the May budget of last year when the finance minister said that the Canadian economy will generate more than 250,000 new jobs "this year". Previous ministers of finance used that kind of rhetoric. Creating 250,000 new jobs each year sounds noble enough, until you remember that in the past three years the labour force has grown at well over
300,000	people a year.
With respect to employment measures, the Minister of Finance in the last budget did not mention any moves the government would take to reduce the jobless rate. When I spoke in the last budget debate I said, if I may quote myself, that this government is resigned to going through the rest of this year with unemployment at about 7 per cent of the labour force. Obviously, I was mistaken. We now know that the government is resigned to 8 per cent unemployment, and next year the figure could be higher.
The main features of last May's budget were measures to increase the qualifying period for those on unemployment insurance. This is typical of the kind of economic leadership we have been getting from the government. Each time the unemployment rate goes up, the government toughens the Unemployment Insurance Act. The government believes that the number of claimants on unemployment insurance should remain static, regardless of what the actual unemployment rate is. Successive ministers of manpower and immigration have been heavily influenced by those in the country who see the increased costs of unemployment insurance in terms of more people ripping the system off. These people fail to realize that increased jobless figures will naturally inflate the cost of providing benefits to the unemployed. This is something I do not believe I have ever heard the minister say. I do not think he has the courage to say that.

Recent press reports have suggested that certain corporate leaders have asked the Minister of Finance to decrease corporate taxes as a measure to stimulate the economy. I only hope that this approach is rejected by the Minister of Finance. Past budgets should have convinced him once and for all that these types of measures have had a spectacular lack of success.
A former member of the Liberal cabinet, Mr. Eric Kierans, said last September that he doubted any nation in the world has given its corporate one thousand persons or industries a more handsome gift package of subsidies, tax allowances, two-years write-offs, cheap loans and the like than our present government. In view of this, and in view of the fact that past reductions in corporate taxes have done little to increase employment, the Minister of Finance should reject these pro: posals outright.
As I mentioned, previous actions by the government give little hope that any future actions taken by it will resolve some of our economic difficulties.
The New Democratic Party has laid down certain proposals which would lead to full employment. We know that this would not happen overnight, and we admit that, but at least we know that those proposals would lead to full employment. We know this objective of providing a job for each man and woman who wants one is not an objective of the government. The present economic situation attests to that. At the same time we know that the government does not have as one of its objectives the reduction of the inequality which exists in this country.
Figures on income redistribution released by Statistics Canada and published in the Globe and Mail on February 22 show that the poorest fifth of families received 7.1 per cent of after-tax income compared with 37 per cent for those in the top 20 per cent of income earners. The figures show that there has been little improvement in the inequality of income distribution during the past decade, despite all the programs of the government. The lack of economic leadership in Canada has left the poor in exactly the same position they were in ten years ago.

speechtext: Marginally worse.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
And as my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), says, marginally worse. Many people are seriously questioning why, in a country as rich as ours, the unemployment rate is 8 per cent, and why no real efforts have been made to redistribute income. The simplest answer, to my mind, is that the present system confers many benefits upon a small segment of Canadian society.
With respect to unemployment, Robert Lekachman, a professor of economics at the City University of New York, said in a recent article in Harper's magazine that, and I quote:
. . . full employment is ihe most efficient agent of equitable income redistribution which is at all politically feasible.
March 8, 1977

It is for this reason that vested interest groups would prefer to have fairly high unemployment levels. Lekachman further stated:
During periods of high unemployment wages tend to stabilize or remain low and people, scared of losing their jobs, gripe less and even work harder.
Professor Lekachman continued:
During high unemployment periods factory and office workers, alert to potential lay-offs and plant shutdowns, are unlikely to nag unions to make work more interesting and less menacing to health and personal safety.
Professor Lekachman went on to say:
. . . the hunger of communities and regions for jobs and tax revenues has allowed large corporations to extort an endless assortment of valuable concessions either as blackmail to keep existing installations or bribes to lure new ones. Full employment, on the other hand would bring into the labour force men and women who now struggle on welfare and unemployment insurance. Full employment would push wages up for those who are now making less than is required to live on.
What Professor Lekachman was saying was that when there are high rates of unemployment it is beneficial to the employer because he can trade one worker off against another. That is a very important aspect of our economic system today with respect to employment and unemployment.
Professor Lekachman said that a long spell of full employment would substantially narrow existing differentials. The article went on to say that this is unlikely to occur, however, because, and I quote:
. . . These repercussions are severe enough to alarm gentlemen in their clubs and boardrooms.
This particular economist also had something to say about the nation-which this government accepts-that societies must choose between inflation and unemployment. Professor Lekachman destroyed the myth that there has to be a trade-off between employment and the price level. The Phillips curve- familiar to all economists-says that when there is high unemployment it is usually accompanied by low inflation, and conversely, when there is high inflation, unemployment is low. As we have seen in recent years, this is simply not the case any more. Our present rates of inflation and unemployment are both high, yet the Minister of Finance still carries on as though the Phillips curve is theoretically sound.
"Stagflation" is created mainly as a result of the concentration of market power in our society. Here again the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) acknowledged the effects of the concentration of power during his celebrated discussion two years ago, but to date he has done nothing to curb this concentration of power.
Full employment can be achieved without inflation provided effective and selective price controls can be administered. As we have seen, the government is committed to neither. That is why my party introduced this motion, and that is why I am speaking tonight.
I want to make just one or two more remarks before my time runs out. I assume that most hon. members, as I do, call back at night constituents who telephone their constituency offices. Tonight I telephoned a constituent whose wife works in a garment factory in my city of Brantford. Believe it or not, if
Economic Policy
an electric, automatic or mechanical needle goes through a finger or pierces a bone, the injured person cannot leave the factory for doctor's assistance until the end of his or her particular shift.
I was astounded when the person who telephoned me told me that if these employees want to get a glass of water, they have to pay five cents for a styrofoam cup into which to put the water. I wonder how many hon. members would say nothing if every time they went out to the opposition lobby or the government lobby to get a cup of coffee they had to pay five cents. Even on our earnings I wonder what they would say. Hon. members can imagine what these people think when they want a glass of water. I am not going to mention the plant, and I am certainly not going to mention the employee because she would be very conveniently laid off at the end of the week if I did. However, this astounded me.
Why is it then, we ask ourselves, that some people do not want to work in some jobs when they have to pay a lousy five cents just to buy a styrofoam cup so they can get a glass of water? This is the kind of thing we have to clear up.
I support the motion. The government will probably come up with a few goodies on March 31.1 understand there is some movement afoot to put on a full scale TV extravaganza so that the minister, with his few little goodies, can go across the nation into everybody's living room, and people will think it is just great, they are televising the debates in the House.
Let me tell you one thing. Budget debates come, budget debates go, and today we have still-in fact 1 should not say "still"-we have more than one million Canadians out of work.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 know honourable members will agree with me that housing is a social concern, and that the need of all Canadians for affordable housing suited to their needs is a subject which is most appropriate on an opposition day. I want to thank members of the NDP for bringing this subject up because it gives me occasion to bring forth, as parliamentary secretary, some of the things which the department has been doing.

1 think that one of the important roles of the government in the housing sector is the help they can provide to influence the production and the distribution of housing units according to the needs. This was one of the great priorities of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs last year. I think we were quite successful in shifting the production of housing from high-cost to moderate- or medium-cost units. We tried in particular to stimulate the construction of moderate-cost housing.
We have been trying to convey this message for over a year at the federal level. We forecast that we would have a demand-oriented market and that purchasers would be interested in moderate-cost housing. We had warned the residential construction people concerned that those who would do business

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
would be precisely those who would sharpen their pencils and start producing for the market of moderate-cost housing.
We told anyone interested that federal support was concentrated on good housing at moderate prices, and this is where we operated, Mr. Speaker, namely in the area of the Assisted Home Ownership Program.

Although our activities in the housing field have been designed primarily to ensure that Canadians remain among the best-housed people in the world, we cannot overlook the stimulus effect of new construction on the economy of the country, and on employment, as I shall outline in a few moments.
Hon. members will recall that in November of 1975 the minister responsible for housing at that time, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), introduced a series of measures designed to meet the demand for more affordable housing and to assure an adequate level of new production. These measures were incorporated in a four-year strategy known as the Federal Housing Action Program. We set a target of one million new homes to be produced by the end of 1979, to fill an estimated need based on known demographic and other factors.
The first year of the program proved to be successful even beyond our expectations. We had set a target for 235,000 starts, and the industry, responding in important measure to the stimulus of the Federal Housing Action Program, produced more than 273,000 starts-a volume that was greater than during any other year in the country's history.
One of the most important features of these initiatives is the revised Assisted Home Ownership Program, better known as AHOP. In effect AHOP assists home buyers by reducing the initial effective interest rate to eight per cent, as long as the new dwelling falls within established maximum price ceilings. These maximums naturally vary from region to region to stay in line with local market conditions for modest housing.
AHOP harnesses private capital in that first mortgage loans are made by approved lenders at market rates. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation then provides an interest-reducing loan, in the form of a second mortgage, which results in an effective initial mortgage rate of 8 per cent. This rate graduates upward to market rates during a five-year period.
It is important to keep in mind that for the first five years of this mortgage-reducing loan, interest does not accrue. Interest starts in the sixth year, and the repayments on the loan begin the seventh year. This unique procedure allows a Canadian to buy a new home on the basis of future income growth, which is of obvious importance at a time when house prices have escalated so rapidly.
There were many aspects of last year's housing production that provide encouraging signs for the future, and the results of AHOP were among them. The home buyer interest in AHOP confirmed our belief that people want good, moderately priced housing, and will buy it when it is made available.

Starts under AHOP went beyond expectations, with some
37.000	approvals. Most significantly, about 60 per cent of the
64.000	NHA-approved loans for new home ownership were for units below the AHOP price limits and therefore qualified for the interest-reducing loan.
We were most pleased that we were able to announce yesterday that the Ontario Home Ownership Made Easy Plan has been integrated into AHOP to offer increased financial assistance to a wider range of lower income Ontario home buyers.
Now, in Ontario, qualified purchasers who take the maximum AHOP federal assistance-which is the interest-reducing loan plus a subsidy of $750 in the first year of ownership- may now apply for an additional grant of up to $750 from the province. This integrated plan will reduce minimum annual income requirements for qualified Ontario purchasers by as much as $2,500 below existing levels.
Another feature of the federal action program is the Assisted Rental Program, which is also known by its initials- ARP-which was introduced to encourage the production of moderate cost rental accommodation.
As hon. members well know, for some time there has been a serious shortage of affordable rental accommodation in most urban areas of Canada, and rental units produced in recent years have not been sufficient to ease the shortage. At the end of last year, the vacancy rate in Canadian urban areas stood at a very tight 1.3 per cent.
CMHC assistance under ARP is designed to ease the builders' cash flow problems during the early years and provide a reasonable return on equity so they will be encouraged to produce more badly needed apartment accommodation.
The results under the first year of ARP operation was an increase of 15 per cent in rental production over the previous year, to 88,600 apartment units. We expect to see more rental construction this year, now that builders are aware that they can realize a fair return from rental units put up with the assistance of ARP. We anticipate an easing in the rental vacancy rate this year, partly because of an expected increase in apartment construction, and for another reason as well.
Residential building activity was at a high level as we turned into 1977 and, in addition, the volume of approvals for new construction towards the end of the year was at an almost unprecedented level. Inventories of newly completed units will therefore be high during most of 1977, and much of it will be in multiple unit dwellings.
At the end of January, for example, there were about 19,000 newly completed but unoccupied housing units in Canada. More than 11,000 of these were multiple-unit dwellings.
A large number of these multiple-unit dwellings-about 60 per cent-will be for sale as condominiums, and the rest will be for rental, but in either case, the primary market will be people who are now renting accommodation. This is expected to free a significant number of rental units in urban centres, and assist in easing the vacancy rate.
March 8, 1977

Although we tend to emphasize the need for new housing, which is obviously our first consideration, we cannot overlook the continuing importance of conserving present stock-particularly in the older areas of our towns and cities. A home that is preserved and restored, and given at least an extra 15 years of life, is just as useful as a new home, although it will not show up in the statistics on starts. I can recall a favourite expression of the former minister of urban affairs. When he used to attend our briefings he would come in and say, "A save is a start". I think that is a pretty good cliche.
The Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program-better known as RRAP-provides financial assistance for the restoration and repair of dwellings in designated areas. Last year the popularity of this program went far beyond our expectations. We had budgeted for $60 million for RRAP-four times the budget amount of the previous year-and even then we began to run out of money in September. More funds were channelled into the program to meet immediate requirements. For this year a total of $107 million is available for RRAP, which should go a long way toward meeting requirements.
I am pleased at the enthusiasm shown for this program, because in cities and towns across Canada there are many fine homes that can readily be preserved. By doing so, we not only retain needed housing stock, but help preserve the character and dignity of older areas in our cities and towns.
RRAP in itself creates excellent employment opportunities, as hon. members can realize when they consider that about 15,700 houses were rehabilitated under this program last year, thereby creating a good demand for local trades and encouraging seasonal employment. This year we expect an additional 22,500 housing units will be restored under RRAP, providing even more employment opportunities.
Federal housing activities administered through CMHC cover an extremely wide territory. I will not take the time of hon. members to go into further detail on individual programs, but I think it is important in the context of employment creation to realize that residential construction creates jobs directly, through manpower needed in the building trades, but indirectly as well, through businesses that cater to homeowners, such as appliances and furnishings. We cannot overlook, either, the manpower needs of firms that provide the infrastructure, building the sewers, the drains, and filling other servicing requirements.
I have spoken today on only a few of the recent initiatives of the federal government in the housing field, but I have deliberately not touched on one of the most important mandates of CMHC, which is to provide suitable housing for people who require the most help in obtaining shelter, the poor, the sick, the elderly, and others who cannot sustain themselves without assistance. All hon. members are so familiar with the programs that provide assisted housing-directly and in co-operation with provinces, municipalities and non-profit organizations-that they do not need to be reminded of our extensive activities in this field.
Economic Policy
1 should like to mention, though, that the thrust of the federal housing action program was to utilize private capital rather than taxpayers' dollars in the production of residential housing, allowing public resources to be used directly on behalf of Canadians in greatest need, those who are socially and economically deprived.
The federal initiatives in housing have had a significant impact on employment, an impact that cannot be measured in its entirety because it reaches into so many fields. We do know, however, that the federal housing action program meant at least 35,000 additional jobs in Canada last year-jobs that would not otherwise have existed in residential construction and in all of the businesses and industries affected by housing. Further, it is estimated that the four-year program will involve more than one million man-years of employment.
I do not think there can be any doubt, Mr. Speaker, that federal initiatives in the housing field are not only meeting the real needs of Canadians for good, affordable housing, but continue to create a large volume of productive jobs while, in general, adding stimulus to the economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE ECONOMIC LEADERSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate tonight and will centre my remarks around the second section of the motion before us which refers to reducing taxes for middle and low income earners. The people who fall in that category as much as any other class of our society are the farmers of Canada. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has set out the position of this party very clearly and has mentioned our hopes for what will be contained in the budget of March 31.1 wish to elaborate on only one point, the capital gains tax as it relates to the farming community.
Time and again I have put forward proposals to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that would help alleviate the crippling effect of the capital gains tax on farmers. This has come into sharp focus in the riding I represent and in the regional municipality of Haldimand-Norfolk. The reason is that there has been a large land assembly program undertaken by the provincial government which has purchased sites for a satellite city in the former township of Townsend and in the former township of South Cayuga.
In addition, farm land has been taken over by three important industries which have placed themselves in the centre of a rural farming community. Stelco is moving its plant from Hamilton to the south shore of Lake Erie; adjacent to that Texaco is building its largest oil refinery in North America, and Ontario Hydro already has the largest thermal station in Canada located in this area. As a result there has been a great demand for land, and thousands upon thousands of acres of farm land have been sold. At this point farmers came to the full realization of the crippling effect of the capital gains tax.
Let me show by actual example how this works. The selling price per acre of farm land in the general area I speak of was $2,000. The V-day value set by the auditors or the land appraisers of the Department of National Revenue was $300
3786

March 8, 1977
Economic Policy
per acre. That means a total capital gain of $1,700 per acre, half of which, $850, is taxable. The average size of a farm is 200 acres so that means a capital gain of $170,000. If we take a farmer who makes about $10,000 a year and add that, we are talking about a taxable income of $180,000. The rate of tax will then be determined by the tax bracket which is appropriate. The result is devastating, and dozens and dozens of farmers have come begging for advice on how to survive.
The problem usually arises with the determination of a fair V-day value. It is determined largely by the appraiser sent by the Department of National Revenue, and unfortunately most of them have learned their jobs from textbooks and have no farming experience or background. They do not know the real cost of operating a farm, or what is the value of the land. If the farmer had foresight he had the land valued before December 1, 1971, so he knows what the V-day value is-providing the land appraiser he hired is acceptable to the Department of National Revenue. If he and the department cannot agree, he can approach the tax appeal court-where he is confronted with the same land appraisers hired by the Department of National Revenue. Finally he can go to the law courts, and of course this costs money. In my area some farmers band together and share the legal costs of a test case on the capital gains tax.
What options are open to the farmer faced with this problem? If he is on the edge of retirement or can retire and sell his farm he looks to the proceeds as his retirement pension. It is traditional in farming circles for the proceeds of the sale of the farm to provide the retirement pension or superannuation for the farmer. Over the years he has not had sufficient income to make an annual contribution to a pension fund. Therefore he follows the course I have just mentioned. Every cent earned by the farmer has gone toward improving his farm for the time when he will sell it.
What other option is open to him? He can sell the farm, as I suggested, and set up a pension fund. He has no opportunity to establish a registered retirement savings plan in addition to the one I mentioned. He has to struggle for efficiency in order to survive in this day of rising input costs for farmers. He takes all his profit, loans and mortgages in order to modernize his farm buildings and buy equipment, trying to keep pace with rising farm costs and the need to be more and more efficient in order to survive. Everything he has is tied up in his farm.
The capital gains tax is enforced in the case I mentioned and the figures I quoted. It leaves the farmer with no pension except the paltry benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. This is especially true if he has used the proceeds of the sale to purchase another house in which to live out his retirement. It is a sad situation.
One option open is to retire. If he is young, middle-aged or less, and wants to buy another farm, what happens with the capital gains tax? He may not really want to retire or sell his farm but is forced into it by the threat of expropriation. He would rather stay where he has farmed all of his life. Being

forced to sell, he expects to use the proceeds of the sale to pay for a new farm and relocate there. Again his hopes are dashed for the reasons 1 have mentioned.
Capital gains goes to our revenue offices across the country. The cost of relocation requires a heavy mortgage again. What really happens is that at middle age or later he has to start again to build up a farm. It is grossly unfair.
So much for the problem, what about the solution? One answer, and I proposed this many times to the Minister of Finance, is that there be a once in a lifetime exemption for the sale of a family farm without attracting capital gains tax.
In 1970 and 1971 when the tax reform legislation was being debated in this House of Commons, we in this party argued forcibly and logically that farms be exempt, period. The government was adamant, saying they must be taxable for capital gains. It continues to hold that position to this day. It did make one small concession. The tax department agreed that a sale of a farm from father to son, where the farm would continue to be operated as a viable farm enterprise, would be exempt.
I personally made the proposal that there be a once in a lifetime exemption on the sale of a family farm. I would include in that an incorporated farm enterprise where the holders of the shares of this company are father, son, mother and other members of the family. This would permit retirement with dignity on a pension the farmer has paid for by the sweat of his brow. It would also permit relocation if that were desired.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a submission to the Minister of Finance in February of this year. On page six, item two, they underline the point I have been making. They say, and I quote:
The objective of improvement of farm productivity, rationalization of land use, and preservation of the family farm structure of enterprise are very ill-served by the present law which, except in the case of involuntary sale as in expropriation, require that a farmer realize and pay tax on capital gains if he wishes to sell assets such as a portion of his farm to buy another better located parcel, or to intensify his enterprise by making investments in buildings for livestock production on the remaining portion of his land.
This is a very important matter. Cases have been brought to our attention where two farmers are practically unable to make an exchange of land even though both would benefit because the exchange would trigger the capital gains tax which neither should have to pay on such a transaction. Sometimes the exchange does not take place and one or both of the farmers leave the business. This results in the encouragement of large land holdings by those better able to purchase the land.
The second problem I want to draw to the attention of the minister is the inflation factor which should be used in calculating capital gains from V-Day value up to the date of the sale. The real value of the property has not increased to the amount that I mentioned in my example, $170,000. The increase is largely due to inflated land costs, particularly in the area I represent, and I believe this holds true all across this
March 8, 1977

country. Some consideration should be given to the inflation factor so that a percentage could be deducted for that reason.
The increase in capital gains is largely illusory. I again refer to the submission which I quoted a few moments ago. 1 quote from page seven, item three:
It is of course as clear as crystal that in an inflationary economy some or all of capital gains represent illusory gains in real terms because of the declining real value of money. It continues to be the policy of the federation that the taxation of such illusory gains is confiscatory and should not be permitted. This position we would note is being increasingly supported by the business community, and recently by the Joint Taxation Committee of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants.
That is a very reasonable suggestion. The Minister of Finance would do well to take heed.
The third proposal would be an assignment of land value each year into a registered retirement savings plan. Rather than make a parallel explanation, I will simply quote again the brief by the CFA, pages seven and eight, item four. This would give the farmer an opportunity to build up a registered retirement savings plan which, as 1 said a few moments ago, is most difficult for him to do under present conditions. I quote:
In general of course when a taxpayer invests in a retirement savings plan he has to save out of his income sufficient money to make that investment. This is very advantageous from an income tax point of view, and most taxpayers are not too severely restricted in the sort of investment that they may choose to make. A farmer, however,'is typically under constant pressure to make additional investment in his farm to maintain its technological efficiency and economic viability. This severely limits the ability of farmers to take advantage of the tax deferral benefits of investment in registered retirement savings plans, and also reduces the amount he may make available from his income for investment, because it must be an after-tax amount.
We would propose that to correct this situation a special provision be made that would permit the farmer to obtain tax deferral, if he wished to do so, by assigning part of the value of his land each year (up to $5,500) to a registered retirement savings plan account. The existence of the deferred tax obligation involved could be registered as a lien on the land so that it could not be sold or transferred without automatic notice to the tax authorities.
We would propose that the value of the RRSP account would at any time be simply the aggregate of the amounts of money assigned to that account, up to $5,500 per year, so that for example if $5,500 were assigned for 10 years the value of the farmer's retirement plan would be $55,000 and would be taxable as income if realized unless invested in an annuity or the amount invested in another plan. Under such an arrangement we would see no need for a procedure to determine if the amounts credited to the plan were actually invested in the farm enterprise. It should be provided that the farmer could at any time, if funds became available to him to do so, reduce or dissolve the special RRSP account by investing part of the amounts in that account into another RRSP. In the event of the death of the farmer, the RRSP could be inherited by the spouse, or if by others would become payable.
It would be our expectation that such a provision would be used sparingly by farmers, in fact, but that it would be exceedingly useful to some-especially young farmers with heavy investment requirements.
This outlines a proposal to give the farmer the benefit of an RRSP which he does not presently enjoy.
One other item I should like to draw to the minister's attention has to do with the capital gains tax especially as it affects farmers who sell their quotas or, in my area, where they grow tobacco, their marketing board rights on tobacco land. In the Income Tax Act this is discussed in what is referred to as the "nothing section". But when the rights are
Economic Policy
sold they become really "something" in the way they attract capital gains tax.
1 am suggesting to the minister that consideration be given to permitting a farmer to use the income received from the sale of these quotas or rights to purchase equipment to serve him in a new enterprise on his farm. For example, instead of growing tobacco or shipping milk, he might grow corn. The proceeds from the sale of the quota could be used, in that case, to buy storage equipment, drying equipment, combines and so on. Thus he would be able to make use of the roll-over provisions of the act. At present he cannot do so, and I suggest to the minister that the hon. gentleman find ways of making this possible.
In conclusion I would point out that the budget coming up on March 31 offers the Minister of Finance an excellent opportunity to give effect to some of the proposals I have made from time to time in the House, and which I am making again tonight.
I might add that what I have said about the family farm applies equally to small businesses operated by a family. The small businessman plows back his earnings into his business in the form of new equipment, the remodelling of his shop or store, and when the time comes for him to retire or sell his business, he too hopes to use the proceeds by way of a retirement pension. The capital gains tax deprives him in the same manner of the support in his retirement he might otherwise have enjoyed. I respectfully suggest that both for the farm community and the small businessman the minister should provide some relief in his upcoming budget.

Much has been said this evening about the performance of the Canadian government in managing the Canadian economy. I think I can say to those assembled here tonight that the government has done an incredible job in managing the economy over the difficult period we have been through in the last few years. Throughout industrialized nations we have seen in the last few years an absolute stagnation if not a decline in their gross national products. Our own has been nothing to crow about, but when we look at the figure in narrow terms we are bound to consider the growth, or lack of growth, of the Canadian economy in relation to the performance in other countries around the world. I say the government has done a first rate job and it puzzles me why the opposition cannot admit that it has done an incredible job in managing the economy.

Perhaps I should not pay so much attention to the ribald comments from the other side. At any rate, if I have time I will return to the subject of transit aid, though I hardly think it bears repetition in view of the statements made by my hon. friends and myself in the past week.
One of the means the government has employed to cushion the blows of inflation, to restrict the harm done by the recession of the last few years, is that of indexing. The hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), who is over there by the curtains, takes a somewhat resentful attitude to this on the ground that it was the Conservative party who put forward this idea. That is Fine. There is nothing wrong in a good idea being implemented if it Finds support among Canadians and contributes to the well-being of the country. Are members on the other side so petty that they would take so selFish a position?
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is bereft of any kind of policy statement. Now we can see how this attitude on the other side has developed. They are sore because a good idea was implemented. Canadians will ask themselves: is this the kind of party to which we ought to entrust the government of the country? I would say not. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has been around for many years and has been associated with efforts to promote the cause of old age pensioners, medicare, good unemployment insurance legislation, a non-discriminatory immigration bill, and so on. I do not hear him bemoaning the fact that the Liberal government which has instituted so many of these progressive policies got its ideas originally after some prompting from members of his party. They are grateful, I am sure, that they were put into legislative form by the Liberal government for the benefit of all Canadians.

Ideals are Fine. Ideas are Fine. But they constitute only part of the political process. It is not good enough to have ideals and ideas without a vehicle for their practical application. In this respect I suggest that the Liberal party is a model, not only for this country but a model for parties in other democratic countries, on the basis of its performance over the past year or so. We have ideas and ideals. We have been flexible. We listen to public opinion. We put these into legislative form for the benefit of all Canadians, so there must be something right about that approach because we have been returned many times to give leadership to the nation.
To demonstrate my very impartial and gentle nature, I want to give the hon. member for New Westminster a chance to get on the record tonight. After all, this motion was put forward by his party. But before I sit down I want to talk about the unemployment statistics which have been bandied about in this House.
In the last month the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), the leader of the NDP, has been talking about the scandalously high unemployment which is verging on 10 per cent-the hidden unemployment. I am not debunking the fact that we do have a serious unemployment problem in this country, but we should analyse statistics properly. Statistics can be manipulated for one's own ends. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has been very effective, I think, in criticizing the approach of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has left the Chamber now; I guess he did not want to stay for the rest of the debate.

As 1 was saying, there are different kinds of unemployment. Take, for example, someone who leaves school, who lives in Thunder Bay or Sault Ste. Marie, who gets a job 50 miles away in a less popular part of the country, and who does not want to move. He is counted as unemployed.
March 8, 1977

Then there are many women in our work force who work not simply for economic reasons, though the economic benefit is appreciated, but also for self-fulfilment. The families of these women do not need a second income, but if they are laid off or they choose to leave their job they are designated as looking for work and become part of the unemployment statistics.
I should like to pay particular tribute to a very incisive analysis of this particular problem-the absolute manipulation and distortion of unemployment statistics by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby-by Mr. Jack MacArthur, the business editor of the Toronto Star. Those of us who represent Toronto ridings have not been too kindly dealt with during the past few years by the Toronto Star, and sometimes 1 shudder when 1 open the editorial pages. Mr. MacArthur is not a person who is a defender of the government in the absolute sense, but he is a very discriminating and perceptive analyst and journalist who criticizes where necessary and gives credit where necessary. I would advise members on the other side, especially those in the NDP, to read his article which appeared in the Toronto Star for February 10 last in which he talks about high unemployment and low unemployment being the same thing.
Paragraph three of the motion before us asks the federal government to assist urban communities financially to ensure an immediate expansion of municipal capital works projects, including rapid transit. My views on rapid transit are pretty well known. This kind of clause is very similar to one introduced in the House by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), I think before Christmas. It is the old chestnut that keeps coming up, namely, that the federal government should forgo the federal sales tax on municipal purchases, the basic argument being that this is a tax upon a tax. That may well be so, and in participating in debate on the hon. member's motion I gave him credit for bringing this point to our attention.
There are a number of anomalies and problems with municipal financing. In the province of Ontario the provincial government has appointed a commission, under Mr. Willis Blair, a former mayor in part of my constituency, to look into the property tax base. Mr. Blair is suggesting, among other things, that federal and provincial buildings-I am not sure whether he mentioned the churches, but buildings that do not pay taxes-should be taxed to increase municipal revenue. Like the motion of the hon. member for Vegreville, this is again a half-hearted, piecemeal approach.
Any fundamental discussion of federal assistance for municipalities has to be organized within the context of the constitution of this country. We have to redraw provincial and federal responsibilities. We have to rethink our financing. Until we are prepared to do that, and until the provinces are prepared to sit down with the federal government and talk about overlapping jurisdictions and more equitable sharing of revenues, I do not think we should be jumping in with one foot. We should think out the whole problem very seriously.
I did promise that I would sit down and give the hon. member for New Westminster an opportunity to say his piece. I see there are ten minutes left and I should just like to
Economic Policy
reiterate some of the comments I made on urban transit. It may be argued, and it is argued by my colleague for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), that the federal government has no constitutional jurisdiction to fund urban transit systems. This is a particular point of view. 1 do not believe that this is a fiat which is written in tablet form or inscribed in stone for all time. This is a matter that should be discussed within the confines of a federal-provincial conference on the new constitution.
In 1974 we did make certain promises. If the government is going to have any credibility with people in the urban areas, especially in metropolitan Toronto, which includes an area which I happen to represent, we must at least have some attention paid to partially discharging these promises. We should not have a kind of open-ended program which will drag on for years and years, a cost sharing program like medicare where the federal government writes a blank cheque and the provinces go on spending money ad infinitum. But perhaps we should have a three or five year commitment by the federal government to have money available to encourage municipalities to develop public transit systems.
I am not going into all the arguments in favour of public transit and why it should be encouraged. However, I would agree with the motion in that the government must, in its budget, give some financial commitment and must put in practical form some of the promises that were made in 1974. I realize the problem of financial restraint which the government has. As I said last week, the government has done a very effective job in putting a clamp on the growth of government expenditure, and should be applauded for that.
The second paragraph of the motion speaks of reducing taxes for middle and low income earners. I agree this is a very laudable suggestion and I hope that the Minister of Finance includes it in his remarks on March 31.
The first paragraph of the motion was dealt with very effectively by my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and I do not propose to comment further.
As the House can see from my remarks, the three parts of the motion do not seem to be too unrealistic. However, it is the preamble to this whole discussion which upsets me. As I have said, it gives further evidence of the self-righteous or pious approach which is so typical of the NDP, and is the principal reason that I cannot support the motion in this form.
I have much more to say, but with true parliamentary courtesy I will yield the floor to the hon. member whose party proposed the motion originally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider that as a promise, although it sounded pious and self-righteous. Let me return to the substance of the motion, which deals not only with rapid transit but with housing as well.
As a nation we are short of energy. We are spewing energy into the air every day, wasting it. Surely, considering that one million of our people are unemployed, and six million of our
[Mr. Leggatt.)
housing units not properly insulated, we could put people to work across the country insulating houses. That program would (a) cut down the waste of energy, and (b) put people to work. The government has made a slight move in that direction, for which we give it credit. It has started an insulating program in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. That program must be extended across the country. Many members of this House, no matter where they sit, would support that program. Therefore we urge the government to come forward in the forthcoming budget with a meaningful employment program directly related to problems of energy waste.
Let me now touch on municipal works projects. Frankly, all in this House are sick and tired of make work projects not doing the job. Let me give you an example. We have 145,000 unemployed tradesmen in Canada, or one out of seven, according to latest Statistics Canada figures. Yet through LIP, Canada Works, and Young Canada Works we are creating jobs which those unemployed tradesmen could do. For example, they could rebuild the dock in white Rock. All kinds of projects are going on, and skilled tradesmen are anxiously awaiting for their chance to work on them. But instead of working, many of them are drawing unemployment insurance. That is putting our priorities in the wrong order.
The answer is capital works projects at the municipal level, municipally administered. Both labour and capital ought to be administered municipally, in municipal projects right across Canada. We do not need the involvement of the federal bureaucracy. We could do thousands of things in our communities; the free enterprise sector of our economy has not done them, obviously because there is no profit in them. I do not blame free enterprise; I understand the system. But, as a nation, we could undertake some of these projects.
We could undertake a project in my own riding, for instance, to clean up the fishing bars on the Fraser River. We could pull all of the stumps. We could build tremendous parks all along the Fraser River. That make work project could last for five years. But we do not do this because of ideological shortsightedness, because it is not profitable and because, as I say, free enterprise will not tackle it. Surely the government ought to be active in this area. Its involvement would create enough employment to put a significant dent in our unemployment statistics.
My party is often accused of being anti-business. I tell you that our proposal to reduce taxes for the middle and low income earners would be the best break business in this country could ever get. If accepted, it would increase purchasing power. The little guy would get a break and use his purchasing power to buy what he needs. I hope these appeals are not falling on deaf ears. I am delighted to see the minister present; I know he listens carefully. I understand that we are to see a gun bill very shortly; I hope he is not going to give in to the snipers' lobby. We are not sure. We hope there will be some teeth in the bill.
I want to emphasize how beneficial would be a reduction of taxes at the low end of the income scale. We often wonder how to put purchasing power in the hands of low income people.
March 8, 1977

The answer is obvious. We have allowed people to deduct their political donations from tax payable. That is great for people interested in politics. Why cannot we do the same for low income families, and allow them to take day care expenses off their tax?

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TOLL INCREASES- POSSIBILITY OF COMMITMENT FROM UNITED STATES
TRANSPORT-ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TOLL INCREASES- POSSIBILITY OF COMMITMENT FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) made a significant statement outside the House concerning the debt attached to the St. Lawrence Seaway. This problem has been before us for some time. With his usual political dexterity the minister landed himself in great difficulty in this House because of his decision to make the gist of his statement outside the House. Be that as it may, hon. members learned the details of the statement, and those details have been the cause of considerable discussion. His statement presented to me at least three major questions which I hope can be answered by the parliamentary secretary tonight.
First, the question that brings us here tonight was asked by me on Thursday, March 3. I asked:
How firm a commitment is there from the United States on the proposed St. Lawrence Seaway toll increases, and where did that commitment come from?
Adjournment Debate
I asked that because the minister in his statement outside the House indicated that the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls would be doubled. The Minister of Transport replied:
Mr. Speaker, as the announcement yesterday indicated, the question of arranging these increases by agreement is a matter of negotiation, so it is not a matter at this point of talking about a commitment.
Apparently the matter had not been raised during the visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Washington to call upon the President of the U.S.A.
We are dealing with a substantial sum, the debt of the Seaway, that is, its capital cost, which is generally considered to be around, $642 million. The interest on that debt alone is considered to be at least $200 million, and some members of the House have alluded to the whole problem as being more than a $1 billion problem. But even taking the figures that have been presented on the more conservative side-if 1 may use that statement of my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall)-it would seem to be at least an $800 million problem.
The Minister of Transport in replying to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East said:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the debt is concerned, there are two parts to the debt, the accrued interest which it is not intended to treat as a current liability and in due course to remove,
1 took from that use of language that he meant that this $200 million, or whatever the accrued interest is deemed to be, is wiped out.
The minister went on to say, as reported at page 3571 of Hansard:
and the balance of the debt, the initial construction cost, which it is intended to convert into equity.
He noted later that it was hoped to realize a modest return on this equity, something in the order of one per cent, which would mean that on the $800 million now owing and not retrieved by the tolls that have been imposed on the operations of the Seaway so far, one could hope to get about $6.4 million a year back. It seems to be a very small return on a substantial amount of money, and of course as somebody said it does not begin to represent a proper return on the amount of money that has been invested by the taxpayers of this country and the taxpayers of the U.S.A. Even doubling the tolls, which seems to be a hefty increase, will not bring about anything that will approach Fiscal probity in this particular matter.
The questions I would like to direct to the parliamentary secretary and which will be raised when the department's estimates are before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications are the following: is this going to be a precedent for all transportation in Canada, that the taxpayers put up all the capital and that the return upon that capital turns out to be a laughable figure? Is this the brave new future for transportation in Canada, when we are faced with some rather large transportation problems?
Since the minister told us that it would be a matter of negotiation and not a matter of commitment from the United States, will the Americans agree to this increase? Will they

March 8, 1977
Adjournment Debate
think it is adequate and just? Will they think it should be more? What will their position be? This seems to me to be a very strange way to carry on a partnership. Admittedly this is a very contentious problem, but it is strange that one side should announce what the solution is going to be, apparently without really having discussed the matter with the other side. As I noted earlier, the minister seemed very firm in his statement to me about the fact that there were going to be negotiations and that there had not been a commitment.
The figures presented to us by the minister on that day after his press conference indicated the nature of the increase on the tolls through the Seaway. I represent a port which has had some fights with the minister over the "at and east" rates on flour and grain shipments. It seems to me, with the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls going up to the level the minister proposes, that what the minister has often called his unit train concept of moving grain from western Canada to Halifax and Saint John for shipment abroad will still not be competitive, all other things being equal.

AIRPORTS-PICKERING-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO CONSTRUCTION-POSSIBILITY OF DIVERTING FUNDS TO AID COMMUTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised tonight in the adjournment debate by myself

follows at least 90 oral questions which have been directed to the government concerning the proposed Pickering airport. We have pressed for an answer many times. I myself have put more than 20 questions on this matter. The government has consistently evaded any attempt to take a clear stand or view with respect to this ill-conceived project. The latest round of questions 1 had with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is no exception.
On February 14 I asked the minister whether, in light of the fact that there has been little or no growth in air traffic at Toronto's Malton airport, the government might reconsider its stubborn, but senseless commitment to saddle the country with a white elephant similar to the one it built at Mirabel. Despite the fact that the minister himself admitted that "air traffic had failed to reach projected levels", not just in Toronto but throughout North America, and despite the fact that it had just recently been revealed that Mirabel had lost $47 million in its first year of operation, the minister hedged once again saying only that air traffic had not been reduced significantly.
I asked my question because current statistics show that air traffic in Canada and in many other parts of the world has, so to speak, "plateau-ed out". The government's repeated statements that somehow Malton will become overcrowded do not appear to be backed up by existing statistics; in fact I often suspect that the government, for bizarre reasons known only to itself, based the entire project at Pickering on rather questionable projections in the first place.
The point is this: it is always reprehensible for the government to spend great sums of money on frivolous or dubious projects, but it is especially callous for it to do so when it is openly dickering with the possibility of breaking its election promise to provide $290 million to aid urban transit across Canada.
There is a wide discrepancy among projections for the estimated cost of Pickering. Certainly we know that to date they have spent $110 million; but the lowest estimate, $200 million, is an amount sufficient to finance all the urban transit projects which are currently being jeopardized in Metro Toronto due to the government's reneging on its 1974 promises.
It is inconceivable to me that the government can be oblivious to the fact that there is severe commuter congestion in Toronto while it stubbornly refuses to give up its dream of building a second airport that is not required. It is inconceivable to me that the government can turn its back on 75 per cent of our population who live in our urban centres in order to accommodate the marginal 10 per cent who use airports on a regular basis.
It is time the present administration gave us a candid answer. Will it scrap Pickering and divert the remaining funds to more productive enterprises such as the Toronto terminal improvement project, which is needed to relieve congestion at Union Station? Will it repudiate the remarkable statement made Friday by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister
March 8, 1977

of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) that the people of Toronto should be grateful the government broke its promise? The parliamentary secretary in effect said in that statement that the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1974 had a double advantage; first of all they got the Prime Minister re-elected and, second, now that the Prime Minister chooses to break those promises, somehow he will end up saving people of the Toronto area some money. That is the Alice in Wonderland reasoning put to this House by the parliamentary secretary only last Friday.
I hope the government will come to its senses and say it has agreed to abandon the Pickering project, that it was an unfortunate concept in the beginning, a civil servant's dream and that it now realizes the airport is not needed.
I hope the government will take this opportunity to commit the money earmarked for Pickering for more worth-while developments in the Toronto area, namely, the urban transit which is needed to facilitate people who wish to go to work and who pay taxes in that greatly congested area of Canada.
The time has come when the government must get its priorities straight. For years we have urged it not to plunge money into the development of airports but to put it into more meaningful development that would aid people in getting to and from work. This is the question that I say we have put to the government 90 times: will it reconsider the Pickering development, come to its senses and divert the funds that were to be put into that needless development to a more worth-while project such as urban transit in the Toronto area?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is very difficult to follow in his goal, his financial philosophy, and his administrative approach. As I said in my speech this afternoon, the hon. member in a speech on March 3 asked for more funds in the urban transportation budget. According to his own figure, and it was mentioned tonight, he is asking for his own area a sum of $200 million. If we consider the Montreal area, the Vancouver area and other municipalities, it would take not only millions but a billion dollars. How can the member reconcile those demands, be conscious of the inflation situation, and also be opposed to an increase in the expenses of the federal government, while protesting Treasury Board policy?
First, I would like to clarify the hon. member's mistaken impression that there still exists certain moneys, formerly earmarked for Pickering, which can now be made available for such programs as urban transit.
The 1975-76 estimates included $51,109,000 for expenditures at Pickering. During the preparation of the 1976-77 Main Estimates CATA recognized that only $39,964,000 would be required for 1975-76. Therefore the anticipated unused funds were applied against the revolving fund loan authority, thereby reducing the requirement for new loan authority. The decision to set the Pickering proposal aside in the fall of 1975 resulted in still lower levels of expenditures for 1975-76. This was taken into consideration in the 1977-78 estimates and again served to reduce new loan authority

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-USE OF WRITS OF ASSISTANCE-POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ISSUANCE AT DISCRETION OF JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my participation tonight arises from questions which I raised in the House of Commons on February 21 of this year in connection with writs of assistance which are available in the enforcement of the Customs Act, Excise Act and others passed by this parliament. I also raised the matter of writs of assistance on previous occasions.
I was pleased to hear the minister indicate on February 16 that he shared my concern about some of the powers provided under the Criminal Code and through investigative agencies. I was pleased to have his assurance that he was giving the matter some consideration and in fact had directed the Law Reform Commission to make a study with regard to this whole general area.
I wanted to pursue this matter in the course of the question period on February 21. I asked the minister whether, having had an opportunity to study the judgment of Mr. Justice Collier, he was in a position to give some tangible evidence of his concern by undertaking to recommend changes in the legislation which would have the effect of allowing some discretion by the judiciary in the issuance of writs of assistance in the future.
At that time the minister indicated that he was looking at the matter. However, from his reply I got the impression he was only looking at internal arrangements of his own department and other departments respecting applications for writs of assistance, and determining by internal arrangements what could be done to avoid any abuses.
I am pleased to see the minister here. His presence in the House indicates that this is a matter of some importance. It is certainly regarded as important by the Canadian Bar Association.
The civil liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association has characterized the availability of writs of assistance under the legislation to which I have referred as repugnant. Eminent jurists have commented adversely on this provision, as have lawyers across the country and people generally who are interested in the proper administration of justice and in the preservation of civil liberties. I believe the fact that the minister has stayed up so late this evening to deal with the matter is a reflection of the importance he attaches to it.
My own point of view, and I want to put it on record, is that writs of assistance are a glaring exception to the general rule of Canadian law that judicial authority must be obtained before warrants are issued. This also covers wire tapping. It seems to me the police should not have the authority to obtain writs of assistance which are unlimited as to time and which

It might be simpler in all these circumstances to have the minister himself grant these writs. subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-USE OF WRITS OF ASSISTANCE-POSSIBILITY OF AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ISSUANCE AT DISCRETION OF JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for raising this issue tonight and for his questions in the House on this subject of writs of assistance which, as he says, are an extraordinary legal remedy and a procedure it is incumbent upon us to examine from time to time. I am also grateful to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) who raised this matter with me and with the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) many months ago in correspondence with us.
The immediate issue comes to light as a result of a decision of Mr. Justice Collier in Federal Court very recently, in which he was asked, on the application of myself or my officials, for a number of writs of assistance. I am pleased with the line of argumentation that the hon. member has made which pointed out that these are extraordinary legal remedies, but which called for some requirements as a minimum. I think we want to be careful in a country such as ours, faced with the law enforcement problems that we have, and faced with law enforcement officers often operating in extremely remote areas, that we do not outlaw writs of assistance without careful examination.
While complaining of the total lack of information provided to him as a judge having to issue the writs, a footnote to the judgment of Mr. Justice Collier states:
I am not suggesting writs of this kind should never be asked for or granted. There may be moral, political or social grounds. The material in support of this application, for example, is completely devoid of any facts which might indicate there is some political, moral, social, economic, or administrative ground for granting this particular individual the powers sought.
So even the learned judge, while complaining, I think rightly, about the lack of information before him, conceded that there may well be valid reasons for the exercise of the writs.
In examining the matter one finds that the administrative procedures within departments are such as to endeavour administratively to eliminate abuse. In fact, the administrative procedures are such that a writ is not supposed to be used unless there were circumstances where, if a justice of the peace were available to issue a search warrant, one would in fact be granted.
It is not enough solely to rely upon administrative procedures, and that is the reason that I have said, in the light of Mr. Justice Collier's decision, that no further writs of assistance will be applied for until the whole procedure is reviewed. In saying that I meant not only administrative procedures but legal procedures.
